articles.content:
Winners of the IDFA Forum prizes were announced at an awards ceremony in Amsterdam Wednesday, honoring projects presented in the festival's co-production and co-financing market.

How Love Moves by Pallavi Paul won the Al Jazeera Documentary Co-Production Award, which comes with a $25,000 prize. The award recognizes projects “addressing an urgent issue of our time, presented in the Pitch or Roundtable categories.” How Love Moves is no stranger to the festival: it received IDFA Bertha Fund support through the IBF Classic scheme, in the Development category in 2024 and the Production and post-production category in 2025. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Documentary Cinephil Boards Alexandru Solomon's Romanian Election Doc 'Small Expectations' - IDFA Documentary IDFA Artistic Director Isabel Arrate Fernandez On Festival's Competition Lineups, "Huge" Interest In Elizabeth Holmes Doc, And AI In Documentaries

Jurors Mohamed Elmongy and Brigid O'Shea wrote of How Love Moves , "As the selectors of the Al Jazeera Co-Production award we took carefully into consideration the urgency and relevance of each selected project for IDFA Forum as well as the aesthetic, artistic, and creative qualities they hold. We unanimously agreed to give this award to a politically and creatively sophisticated project, exploring the vulnerability of communities deemed dangerous and wrong through state-inflicted violence. In doing so, we believe audiences around the world will have access to a place and the people living there who otherwise we may never encounter, and correct or add a new layer of complexity beyond the mainstream narrative. And more importantly, it is an exciting opportunity to support a woman-director's voice, we hope at a critical junction in the life of her project." The ARTE European Talent Development Award, recognizing a project in development or early production presented in the Forum's Pitch or Roundtable categories, went to Stitch by Stitch by Alina Baitokova. That award comes with a €10,000 prize.

Jurors Olga Chernykh, Anne-Laure Négrin, and Hanne Phlypo said of Stitch by Stitch , "We were honored to be invited on the jury and listen to so many powerful stories from around the world. We had a long jury deliberation, and many projects were highly appreciated. We recognized the incredible courage of the filmmakers bringing us these stories. If we could, we would have awarded more, and we hope these projects will find their way to be supported, and maybe already found support here at the international market of IDFA." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The jurors continued, "However, as we needed to pick only one project, we decided to award a project from a country whose stories are rarely told, with high need in support right now, and to give a director tools to move the project ahead and tell the story that shows people struggling for their life in a rarely seen part of the globalization. It's a film brought by a promising team, a delicate emerging voice. Therefore, the jury decided to award a film that takes us to Kyrgyzstan, Stitch by Stitch directed by Alina Baitokova, produced by Adilet Karzhoev and Marianna Kaat."

The award for Best Pitch Project comes with a €1,500 prize.

The award for Best Roundtable Project is accompanied by a €1,500 prize.

In other IDFA Forum prizes, the award for Best Rough Cut Project went to Resisting Residents by Nikos Pilos and Arsinoi Pilou.

" Resisting Residents is a powerful reminder of how cinema can champion what we believe in," wrote said jurors Chalida Uabumrungjit and Cleo Veger. "This brave documentary captures a community standing firm for their homes, their dignity, and their right to live together, proving that film can be an essential voice for justice and human solidarity. We were moved by the courage of the residents, who take in newcomers, face their own conflicts and fight eviction together, and by a film team honest enough to show all of it. Shot by a two-person crew living inside the community, it's close, trusting and alive, and we can't wait to see it finished."

The award comes with a €1,500 prize.

Resisting Residents also won the InVision Subtitling Award, presented by Walter Groenewegen, which provides closed captioning and subtitles for a project presented in the Rough Cut category.

The IDFA DocLab Forum Award for Best Project was claimed by This Pleasant Lady by Victoria Mapplebeck. "The jury unanimously agrees that this project is inspirational and addresses serious subjects in an irreverent but impactful way that will engage with audiences no matter of their cultural background or ages. The spirit of the project and the artist fits the vibe of IDFA DocLab. We're also now encouraged to create our own fuck you list!" said jury members Min-Wei Kuo and David Massey.

The award is accompanied by a €1,500 prize.

Jurors additionally recognized Time Hunter XR: Colonial Protocols by Mark Mushiva and Daniel Chein. "The jury want to give a Special Mention to a project that really thinks carefully about how the experience will take audiences on a journey that explores themes of time travel, sci-fi, and embodied archive. The project creates an imaginative and engaging experience that brings forward the perspectives of people whose voices deserve to be heard, and histories that deserve to be told."

articles.content:
Latido Films , a sales agent on Rodrigo Sorogoyen's "The Beasts," Netflix mega-hit "The Platform" and Ventana Sur 2025 breakout "The Whisper," is bringing to market " S.O.S ," a blue sky Caribbean island rom-com which renews Latido's relationship with top Colombian producer Diego F. Ramírez at 64A Films .

"S.O.S." also has a first teaser trailer, shared in exclusivity with Variety . Related Stories Weta FX and TAICCA Partner to Turn Taiwan Into an AI Screen Production Hub for Asia Hollywood Has Flipped on GenAI, Says 'Avatar' VFX House Weta FX Chief: 'If You Don’t Have an AI Strategy, Don’t Bother'

A producer on Sundance hit "Dog Eat Dog," a founding stone in Colombia's modern film industry, Ramírez has gone on to produce one of Colombia's most ambitious non-streamer shows, “Escobar, el Patron del Mal," as well as Toronto premiere "The Dog Washer" and "Killing Jesus," the feature film debut of Laura Mora, director of "One Hundred Years of Solitude." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

In a lighter turn for tougher times, 'S.O.S' weighs in in two ways as a crowdpleaser, a blue sky – literally – comedy, set on an uninhabited Caribbean islet, which also offers the lures of romance and second-chance drama.

In it, Jaime, a once hot-shot photographer, is shipwrecked on the white-sand beach island with Cata and Valeria, the stars of an upcoming telenovela, rated as his country's most beautiful women.

Paradise? The sojourn sets off as hell. Cata, a post peak-fame actress has been reduced to playing the mother of Valeria, an influencer who broke out aping Cata. The two hate each other's guts. Battling to survive, however, all three have to smooth their differences and work together in what morphs into a survival adventure and second chance story where they re-connect with the far more sincere people they once were. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Manuela González (Netflix's ‘Fake Profile') plays Cata, Juan Fernando Sánchez ("La Huésped") Jaime and María Camilo Giraldo ("The Ritual") Valeria.

Fast-paced, but allowing a glimpse of key plot beats, the teaser begins with the shipwreck, flashes back to the photo shoot – "my aunts were your fans," Valeria tells Cata cattily during makeup – then an establishing shot of the isle in the middle of a vast nowhere.

The trio have food at hand, such as a coconut, but they don't know how to open them. time exiled from a community hammock. They build a hammock, but Jaime is banished. They seek refuge in a cave, which is infested by bats.

There is, however, a hint in the teaser's parting shot, however, that love could be in the air between Cata and Jaime.

"S.O.S." is produced by Colombia's 64 Films, headed by Ramírez and Nancy Fernández for 64A Films, with Hans García and Ingrid Cruz for the Dominican Republic's Hannah Films.

"The tone that I'm thinking of is ‘The Blue Lagoon," with the paradisiacal exuberance of ‘Ticket to Paradise,'" said director Nicolas Reyes ("Decisions: Some Win and Others Lose"), also a first AD on the Colombian unit of "Paddington in. Peru."

"For a sales agent, the most interesting and stimulating to be in on a project from its birth, as was the case with 'S.O.S.' said Latido Films Head of International Sales Juan Torres. "The understanding with 64A is remarkable and we are confident this will have a knock-on in the film's commercial results."

articles.content:
EXCLUSIVE : Imax has promoted a pair of executives to newly created roles as it expands its leadership.

Giovanni (Gio) Dolci was named the big screen exhibitor's first chief operating officer, reporting to CEO Rich Gelfond. The executive, currently based in London as EVP and chief commercial officer, will transfer to New York with expanded oversight of Global Theatres and Technology in addition to his current leadership of the Global Sales, and Streaming and Consumer Technology teams.

He'll serve as a key day-to-day strategic partner for Gelfond. Related Stories News Imax CEO Wades Into 'Cliff Booth' Debate: "Frankly, I Don't Understand" News 'The Odyssey' Powers Record Q3 For Imax, Stock Jumps, CEO On Platform's "Power And Potential"

Dolci joined Imax in 2012 as managing director of Europe and Africa and chief sales officer. "Gio has a deep understanding of our business, our partners, and our people at every level. Currently, the Mothership, NCIS: New York , and NCIS : Origins are airing, and come early 2027, NCIS : Sydney will be joining the lineup. Even though it’s exciting that we’re finally going back down under, some fans can’t help but bring up the other shows from the franchise that were unfortunately canceled.

Just this week, he official NCIS Instagram confirmed Sydney Season 4's premiere for this coming January. After that, plenty of people took to the comments to share their thoughts. And not all of the sentiments were positive. Some fans are currently pointing out the sacrifices that have been made to make room for Sydney . That includes cutting Origins ’ third season in half , while both NCIS and newbie New York get full seasons. Others are still hurt over NCIS: Los Angeles and NCIS: Hawai’i 's cancellations, as well as the (still-fresh) cancellation of Tony & Ziva :

As someone who is a fan of every single NCIS show, I’m definitely still hurt over having to say goodbye to these axed shows far too soon. Hawai’i ’s cancellation definitely blindsided me and others, including series star Vanessa Lachey. Quite frankly, I’m still wondering exactly why the Eye Network decided to end it.

As for Tony & Ziva , fans were hoping CBS would pick up the series after Paramount+ canceled it, but unfortunately, that was not in the cards. It's great that co-lead Michael Weatherly is back on NCIS , but it’s still just not the same. Even amid the announcement of the New York spinoff, there were plenty of detractors speaking out about the canceled NCIS shows . While I understand that the network TV is a business, I can still empathize with the sentiments.

Meanwhile, Sydney ’s return marks a change for the franchise that is upsetting fans. Some viewers have been sharing their displeasure over the fact that both Sydney and Origins are not getting full seasons. Instead, the two shows are getting only 10 episodes for their respective seasons. It’s understandable that CBS would do this, given that there’s already too many shows on the schedule, but a 10-installment run just feels way too short.

That being said, I will gladly take what I can get, as a 10-episode order is better than nothing. On that note, I'd imagine that plenty of franchise devotees will continue to tune in for the shows that are still airing. However, I don't expect many of them to stop carrying torches for the canceled shows anytime soon.

At the very least, NCIS: Sydney will finally be returning for Season 4 on Tuesday, January 26 on CBS, streaming the next day with a Paramount+ subscription .

Billy Evans, Holmes’ partner, and Seyfried get into a contentious discussion over dinner about Evans’ attitude toward Holmes. Evans, who has started talking about the box office hit more and more both in interviews and in a Reddit AMA , recently spoke about the visit, and it turns out he didn’t see what was coming at all. In fact, he thought he was extending a peace offering to Seyfried after her portrayal of Holmes in The Dropout .

Seyfried had already been working with Fielder for some time, and over the course of the second half of the movie, it’s clear she was getting more and more frustrated with Evans as she learned more about him. In fact, she was so upset by Evans’ behavior in the footage she had watched with Fielder that was filmed before Holmes reported to prison in 2023, that she expressed a desire to break the couple up. Evans recently told his side of the story to The Hollywood Reporter , saying of the dinner:

It made more sense to me after seeing the film, and hearing her say, ‘I want to break them up.’ I didn’t understand her intentions [when she came over]. I thought we were extending an olive branch and saying, ‘Look, we’re not angry with you. We’re happy to engage. We don’t blame you for your portrayal of Liz [in The Dropout]. You’re an actress, you didn’t write the script, you didn’t develop the story, you didn’t do the research or lack thereof.’

Seyfried’s intentions were never to ask for forgiveness for playing Holmes at this point. At this point, Amanda Seyfried isn't just the actress who portrayed Holmes. She is also an advocate for her. That’s even more apparent when she plays her again later in the documentary, in the recreations of Fielder’s meetings with the former CEO in the Texas prison. Seyfried had, at that point, developed sympathy for Holmes, which is weirdly exactly what Evans was hoping the film would do, though probably not at his expense. Not like this.

It’s impossible to rank all the wildest moments in You Can See Everything . The more I’ve thought about it over the weeks since I saw it, the more each scene stands out from the others. One day I think Evans taking the bowl of eggs out of Holmes' hand is the craziest; other times it's when Holmes seemingly doesn’t understand “Who’s on First?” That’s not even getting into the disputed scene that features Evans in the shower . However, the dinner confrontation is when I was squirming the most in my seat.

Seyfried pulls no punches in telling Evans what she thinks, and in turn, Evans doesn’t hold back his contempt, either. It’s a scene I can’t wait to watch again when I’m finally able to see the movie on streaming, presumably with my HBO Max subscription , soon.

articles.title: Can Peter Rice Fix Netflix? New Content Boss Has a Daunting To-Do List
articles.summary: Ted Sarandos’ handpicked consigliere is tasked with reinventing the streamer — while his boss promises Wall Street that nothing is changing.
articles.content:
Reed Hastings found about Netflix 's big shake-up the same time everyone else did. The Netflix founder (he officially exited the board over the summer) told a rapt audience at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco in late October that the mass layoffs, the exit of content chief Bela Bajaria and the surprise announcement of Peter Rice as its new head of content caught him just as off guard as the rest of Hollywood. "I didn't know those were coming, and it's hard because I'd like to be in the fray helping," Hastings told the audience in the Presidio Theater.

Still, the man who shaped Netflix into today's behemoth had thoughts on what Rice and co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters need to do. "The strategy is doing more and better television shows, more and better movies," Hastings said. "The core brand property is about being thrilling. We realized — it took a long time — that we could be distrusted, we could be disliked, but we can never be boring."

Now the burden will be on Rice to find those thrilling additions to Netflix's menu, perhaps retiring the safe but aging gourmet cheeseburger of the Bajaria era.

Rice helped forge Fox into an entertainment giant and was one of only a few Fox veterans brought into the Disney fold when the assets were acquired under Bob Iger (Disney exec Dana Walden was another). His taste and relationships at both Fox and Disney were, in the words of one source, "exquisite," with a knack for fare that was both commercial and high-end. At Disney, he helped build a general entertainment business from near-scratch, leaning on both FX and Hulu to help it do so.

But he has been out of the corporate mix since Bob Chapek unceremoniously ousted him in 2022, just a few short months before Chapek himself would get the boot.

Those post-corporate gigs, however, shed light on what he can bring to Netflix: He helped the L.A. Olympics Committee develop the entertainment for the opening and closing ceremonies, critical events that will be seen by millions (and perhaps billions) before passing the baton to Kathleen Kennedy. And perhaps more intriguingly, he inked a deal with A24. As A24 was revving up its original productions — thanks to several rounds of investment that ended with a $3.5 billion valuation — the insular New York indie studio signed Rice to a film and TV pact.

It's a testament to Rice's talent relationships that the notoriously director-driven studio tapped him to help shepherd some big swings. His credits at the studio included the Alex Garland-produced Warfare and Chris Rock's return to the director's chair with Misty Green . When he left for his Netflix post, his development slate included A24's biggest production to date, Garland's adaptation of the fantasy video game Elden Ring . In other words, he sought to bridge the highbrow and the mainstream with fare that thrills. It's a skill set that Sarandos seems to admire. "His creative instincts and business acumen are remarkable," Sarandos said to analysts Oct. 20. "Most importantly, Peter Rice understands talent relations."

But Rice will have his work cut out for him thanks in no small part to Sarandos, who keeps a tight leash on Netflix's content output and who already reiterated that the company's content strategy isn't changing. "The business and the business flywheel are working. There's no need for a fundamental shift in strategy," he said, even as he lamented the "doubles and singles" that the company delivered this year. Sarandos wants home runs, and he thinks Rice can do that, with a particular emphasis on the U.S. market.

"These big moves, after a disappointing 2026 in which programming expense grew by 10 percent while U.S. engagement per sub roughly stagnated, admit a problem that is increasingly obvious," Wolfe Research analyst Peter Supino wrote Oct. 20. "Ask a friend whether they are watching more or less Netflix these days — in our experience, they'll say less."

If Rice makes an impact at Netflix in the near term, it may be with the company's film strategy, sources say, with the top job now open with the exit of Dan Lin. Rumors have circulated that ousted Warner Bros. film co-chiefs Pam Abdy and Mike De Luca could be in line to succeed Lin to lead Netflix's film division. But Rice has been telling staff that he isn't hiring a film boss for now. He wants to be in the trenches creatively, multiple sources say.

"We view [the executive changes] as a signal that management is focused on improving content output and creative hit rates," Bank of America analyst Jessia Reif Ehrlich wrote Oct. 21, adding that "management appears increasingly focused on generating larger scale hits in [the U.S. and Canada]. We believe it will take some time before any of the new management changes impact the film or TV slate."

In the meantime, junior executives at Netflix have been calling his former colleagues, asking how to thrive in a Peter Rice meeting. He has strong opinions but can be hard to read. "He'll make you work for it," notes one former colleague of his style, which involves leaving subordinates to figure out the solution without him spelling it out.

While Netflix is a major player in the movie business, it has largely avoided theatrical. Sarandos has said the company has not changed its streaming-first mentality, but rival film executives believe that a year from now, many more of the company's movies will have a theatrical component, à la Amazon.

That's easier said than done. The company has relied on its algorithm — not its marketing — for the vast majority of its successes. But the company has conspicuously changed its tune of late: Netflix users have noticed that it now runs teaser trailers for its shows before other Netflix programming, a classic TV marketing move it has long shunned. And the company launched a major brand campaign dubbed "Find the Thing You Never Knew You Needed" on connected TVs, YouTube, TikTok and other platforms — as well as in movie theaters. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (Nov. 25) and Narnia: The Magician's Nephew (Feb. 12) will be key tests to see if Netflix's marketing department can get people to theaters. Rivals believe they'll need to make more hires with theatrical marketing experience if they want to make a real go of it.

After Netflix failed to acquire Warner Bros. and its library, including DC Comics, Rice will also need to beef up its homegrown IP, particularly on the film side. "Netflix is weak in long-lasting franchises and universes," notes one veteran film exec known for IP plays. "Ted says he wants to have big, culturally impactful successes — and maybe universes. What's then the next chess moves on that? They don't have Marvel or DC, and there's not one big acquisition to do it. How do they navigate that and show Wall Street and the entertainment world they can build what they weren't able acquire?""

Of course, Comcast is set to imminently spin off NBCUniversal, raising buzz in Hollywood as to whether the streaming giant may make one more acquisition play in search of franchises and film expertise. In a note to NBCUniversal staff Nov. 16, CEO Mike Cavanagh touted the "open, partnership-driven approach" that the company has, which "allows us to go even further, bringing great content to consumers wherever and however they choose to engage."

Indeed, one critique of Netflix over the past few years is that some of its biggest hits caught it by surprise, leaving it scrambling to catch up when Squid Game and KPop Demon Hunters hit big. In both instances, the company scrambled to secure Halloween costumes or merchandise for fans, deals that typically would be locked up well before a debut of a series or film. It's a sore spot Sarandos is well aware of. Earlier this year, the co-CEO oversaw the launch of a branding effort dubbed "The Netflix Effect," which attempted to calculate the economic and cultural impact of the company.

"Over the last decade, Netflix shows and movies have consistently shaped what people read, buy, listen to, eat, wear and play. We've pushed old songs back up the musical charts, helped niche sports go mainstream, and boosted sales of everything from chess sets, to Halloween costumes, to home storage," Sarandos wrote at the time. "Now we have a responsibility to keep that flywheel going."

Rice may be able to manage that flywheel better, but "let's only make the hits" is a running joke in Hollywood. Still, Hastings may be on to something. Rice may not be able to guarantee hits, but his track record suggests he can guarantee buzz. Whatever happens next, it won't be boring.

Borys Kit and Aaron Couch contributed to this report.

articles.title: 'SmartLess' Trio to Back 'Small Town Narcos' Podcast (Exclusive)
articles.summary: The partnership with New Metric Media will produce a Chris Kelly-hosted true-crime comedy podcast about Canada's largest drug sting.
articles.content:
SmartLess hosts and creators Jason Bateman, Will Arnett and Sean Hayes are partnering with Canadian indie studio New Metric Media and the CBC, the country's public broadcaster, on a true-crime comedy podcast series, Small Town Narcos, to be hosted by Chris Kelly.

The six-part Canadian series, to premiere globally in Feb. 2027, will center on a 1989 drug sting in the province of New Brunswick, and combine a real-time investigation, interviews with retired Mounties and cartel lawyers, archival materials and dramatic recreations. The podcast will recount two Colombian cartel pilots crash-landing a plane half-filled with Pablo Escobar's cocaine into the New Brunswick woods, only to be arrested by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) after a tip-off and in place to make the country's largest-ever drug bust.

The drama to follow included a foiled jailbreak plot, a daylight assassination, a Supreme Court case argued in secret and an RCMP informant who had infiltrated the cartel. Small Town Narcos , to launch at On Air Fest in Brooklyn, follows on a stable of comedic podcasts from Smartless Media that includes the mega-hit SmartLess , Just Jack & Will, Bad Dates and Owned.

Kelly, while hosting and executive producing the Canadian podcast, is also vp of podcasts at New Metric Media, the producer of Letterkenny and the spinoff Shoresy that has also branched out into podcasts, gaming and other digital media ventures.

"I grew up in a corner of Canada where I was sure nothing exciting had ever happened. Then I found out that for one stretch of 1989, it was the most exciting place on earth. It's like learning your boring parents were secretly spies!" Kelly said in a statement. "As we launch New Metric Podcasts, we're looking to create exactly these kinds of stories – original ideas, distinctive creative voices and unexpected worlds that can connect with audiences in a big way. Small Town Narcos is a great example of what we want to build, and we're excited to bring it to life with our incredible partners at CBC and SmartLess Media."

Small Town Narcos, written by Kelly and Eunice Kim, is produced by SmartLess Media and New Metric Media for the CBC. The executive producer credits are shared by Arnett, Bateman, Hayes, Richard Korson, Bernie Kaminski, Mark Montefiore, Kelly, Chris Okea and Cesil Fernandes, with Kim serving as senior producer.

articles.title: 5 Metropolis Disasters That Make Gotham's Worst Nightmares Look Like a Good Day
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of DC Comics If you ask anyone what the worst city to live in DC would be, odds are that they'd tell you it was Gotham eleven out of ten times. It's true that Gotham has about every problem under the sun and then some, but its horrible reputation actually masks just how terrible it would be to […]

Accurately named, this story was one of the darkest days for the City of Tomorrow. It took place across nine issues of every Superman title in 1994, covering both the “Battle for Metropolis” and “Fall of Metropolis.” To keep it brief, Lex Luthor was inhabiting a clone body that was breaking down, and when he realized that nothing could save him, he decided to unleash his scorched-earth policy to ensure that, if he went down, he'd at least bring all of Metropolis down with him. He set off missiles across the city that reduced most of its buildings to rubble, unleashed killer robots to hunt down any survivors, trapped everyone in visions of their worst fears with a hallucinogenic fog cloud, and even piloted a Kryptonian Warsuit to try and finally bring Superman down.

This is Lex at his most bloodthirsty and destructive , driven by nothing but vanity and a sick sense to leave his mark on the world, even if that be through petty revenge on the people he felt spurned him. Superman, Superboy, and Supergirl managed to save whoever they could, but Metropolis was wrecked like it had never been before or since. As if all of that wasn't enough, Lex wound up making a deal with Neron for a healthy body, so none of this mattered, anyways. One man's tantrum nearly brought down millions of lives, and there's no better story that shows how corrupt but connected Luthor is with Metropolis.

The “Darkseid War” event saw two of the Justice League's greatest villains clash as Darkseid and the Anti-Monitor came to blows, and in the ensuing scramble to save whoever they could, each Leaguer found a path towards divinity. Justice League: Darkseid War – Superman tells about how the newly dubbed God of Strength returned to Metropolis, only to find another alien attacking it to do something with the Man of Tomorrow that remains unclear. However, his weapon was pretty straightforward. After losing to Superman in a fight, the alien infected all of Metropolis with a black ooze that covered and blotted out everything and everyone, leaving them in a kind of horrific stasis. In minutes, it took over the entire city, leaving only Superman.

Superman saved the day, of course, but what this incident really highlights is that alien invasions like this aren't anything out of the ordinary. This wasn't treated like some horrible tragedy that everyone would remember for years, as stuff like this happens in Metropolis all the time. Even Superman calls out how formulaic this type of thing is. Really sit with that. An alien unleashed a black ooze that trapped everyone in the city in minutes, but that's so average that after Superman averts it you just go about your day. The fact that this sort of thing is commonplace in Metropolis says everything it needs to about how absolutely insane its daily life is, and it's nothing good.

This five-part storyline, taking place from Action Comics #1017 to #1021, saw Superman's greatest villains bring war to Metropolis. The mysterious and maniacal Leviathan, the untouchable Red Cloud, and the Apex Lex Luthor and his Legion of Doom joined forces to bring Metropolis to its knees and take over the world, colliding with the Justice League and Young Justice squarely in the middle of the City of Tomorrow. Any one of these heroes and villains could cause some pretty serious damage on their own, but when everyone was throwing punches and lasers at everyone else, it became a bloodbath. Most of Metropolis was left in ruins, and the villains all escaped, meaning that there wasn't even any resolution beyond survival.

This story might not have had the lasting impact that “Fall of Metropolis” had, but it did show just how many players had their eyes set on Superman's fair city. Three distinct groups with their own goals, all able to hold their own or even outright bring down Superman, decided to work together and show everyone that the only thing holding these villains back some days is their own inability to trust each other. If they all worked together, not even Superman would be able to stop them. Everyone has their eyes on Metropolis. It's DC's shining jewel, but that means that everyone wants to own it.

Without a doubt, the biggest and bloodiest battle in this city's history was the Battle of Metropolis. It came about in the pages of Infinite Crisis . Seeing that his plans to create the perfect Earth failed, Alexander Luthor decided to conquer New Earth and remake it in his image. To that end, his Society broke every superpowered villain out of jail and unleashed them like an army on Metropolis, hoping to make it Alexander's first capture in his crusade. Dozens, if not hundreds, of villains appeared in Metropolis with no plan beyond wanton destruction, and so the entire superhero community joined forces to combat them. It would be easier to list everyone who wasn't present for this gargantuan brawl, and you can imagine just how destructive it was.

This fight, just as “Metropolis Doom!” did, showed that Metropolis has become the center point of DC's Earth, with every villain aiming to make it their own. This was about a hundred times more destructive, as it involved far too many characters to name, all pushed to their breaking point long before this actually went down. The battle also served as the ultimate showcase of just how dark comics had become in the Infinite Crisis era, dealing out death and blood like there was no tomorrow, because it treated it like there might not be. This was the costume fight to end all fights, and there's no comparison for just how much it destroyed.

The final Metropolis tragedy is much less impactful and showy than the previous, but is altogether more insidious. Lex Luthor despised Superman for, in his own words, stealing his city from him, so he decided the greatest payback was to prove that Superman couldn't handle everything. Lex unleashed a viral bacteria that infected all of Metropolis but LexCorp and Superman himself, leaving everyone stricken with fevers that would kill them soon enough. He forced Superman to work with Toxin, the Man of Steel's biggest fangirl, to distribute the antidote, but the strain wound up killing her. Superman saved Metropolis, but Lex showed him that his actions would always come at a price that Lex would force him to pay.

This isn't an alien invasion or a massive hero-villain brawl. This is the twisted will of one spiteful man , who chose to risk every life in Metropolis to prove that he could hurt Superman whenever he wanted. Lex can and will use everyone in Metropolis as a pawn for his schemes, all out of some twisted sense of love and ego. Just living in Metropolis makes you a target and potential mark, and Lex is just as powerful today as he was when this was released. Living in Metropolis means living at Lex Luthor's mercy, and there are few things as terrifying as that.

Which of Metropolis's major disasters do you think left the biggest impact on the city? Let us know in the comments below!

Qatar 's Film Committee, the body overseeing the development of the country's film and TV business, is gearing up for the second edition of its Industry Days, running from November 19 to 20 alongside the Doha Film Festival .

The inaugural edition unveiled long-gestated plans with a bang last year. Alongside a 50% film and TV cash rebate, the event also announced plans to shoot a contemporary Barbara Broccoli-produced version of Othello starring David Oyelowo and Cynthia Erivo in the Gulf state as well as partnerships with Neon, Company 3, Miramax, Department M and Sony. Related Stories News Festival In Focus: Qatar Ramps Up International Film & TV Ambitions As Local Talent Shines News Festival In Focus: Doha Gears Up For Lift-Off Against Geopolitical Odds: "It's Not Smaller, We Have More Films & Guests"

On the eve of Industry Days, Hassan Al-Thawadi , Chair of the Film Committee at Media City Qatar and chief architect of its strategy, gives Deadline an update on what happened since and teases the upcoming event. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); }

DEADLINE: What was the feedback after the first edition of the Industry days?

HASSAN AL-THAWADI : The feedback around Industry Days was very encouraging. The first edition gave us an opportunity to introduce our vision for Qatar's film industry, engage the region and hear directly from filmmakers, studios, producers and financiers.

More importantly, after the event, we understood that our vision resonated with support for the ecosystem around financing, production, talent, infrastructure and access to the region we are trying to build.

A year later, our focus is on demonstrating how that vision is taking shape through tangible projects, partnerships and production activity. This edition is about sharing what has moved forward and the progress we have made over the past year, what we have learned, how we have adapted, and what comes next.

DEADLINE: Will this edition feature as many announcements? Can you tease any?

AL-THAWADI: There will be some new announcements, but I will leave the specifics for Doha . The overall message will be very clear: we are moving from vision to execution, building on what we started last year and putting more of the pieces of that ecosystem into place. Ultimately, we are open for business. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Last year was about introducing the Film Committee, our ambition to transform Qatar into a global hub for the film industry, and a new proposition for the region to create greater opportunities and international visibility for Arab cinemas. This year the emphasis is on progress and moving from ambition into activity.

The clearest evidence of progress this year is a portfolio of supported films with Paper Tiger , Artou and Furie s reaching international festivals, and projects moving through creative development and production planning.

You will hear more about the Qatar Screen Production Incentive and how we are extending its regional reach, about projects and talent moving into their next stages, and about partnerships becoming more practical and production focused.

DEADLINE: In the interim, we've had the U.S.-Israel war on Iran which has had fallout across the Gulf region for business and tourism. How has this impacted your plans at the Film Committee?

AL-THAWADI: We can't escape the difficult period our region has experienced. However, the fundamentals of what we are trying to build has not changed. We have a long-term strategy to attract international production, develop Arab talent and capability and to create a stronger platform for stories from our region to reach global audiences.

DEADLINE: Are companies still interested in setting up here or striking partnerships?

AL-THAWADI: Absolutely. We continue to see strong interest, although I think the nature of the conversation has matured. A year ago, much of the discussion was about the proposition of Qatar.

Today, the conversations are increasingly around specific projects, production activity, financing, services and access to the wider region. We are already seeing that translate into production activity through the Qatar Screen Production Incentive, alongside continued engagement with international studios and production partners.

The objective is not simply to have companies establish a presence in Qatar. For us, what matters most is sustained activity: productions being made, capability being transferred, local and regional talent being developed, and commercial relationships that give companies a reason to continue investing and working here and across the region. That is what we are building, and we continue to see appetite for it.

DEADLINE: Have any productions accessed the rebate?

AL-THAWADI: Yes. We have pilot productions already leveraging the Qatar Screen Production Incentive. Three major production companies are currently using the programme, including a leading global streaming platform, and those productions have already created more than 500 jobs locally, while generating activity for hotels, transport, security, logistics and other suppliers.

For us, the important point is that we are beginning to see the incentive translate into real production activity, jobs and opportunities within Qatar, and now we're extending its reach. We are strengthening regional collaboration and building the infrastructure that is required for global studios to film and produce in countries across the region.

DEADLINE: What's the state of play for ‘ Othello '?

AL-THAWADI : We are still in discussions with our production partner, Eon, and look forward to sharing further developments once confirmed.

DEADLINE: What's your long-term view for Qatar's future as a media and entertainment hub?

We believe Qatar can become both a gateway and a platform that serves as regional hub for the global film and entertainment industry: a gateway connecting talent, creatives and companies from our region to global markets, and a platform where international partners can work with the talent, stories and capabilities of the Arab world. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

My long-term view for Qatar as a hub for the global film and entertainment industry continues to be ambitious, expansive and collaborative. Success for us is not simply how many productions shoot in Qatar. It is whether we build a sustainable ecosystem with the necessary financing, production, post-production, distribution, talent development, technology and infrastructure to create lasting cultural and economic value in Qatar and across the region.

Arab storytelling remains underrepresented globally. Our goal is to help create the conditions for those stories to be developed at the highest level and reach audiences around the world, while at the same time making Qatar a serious and trusted destination for international production.

One of the lessons of the World Cup is that when you invest with a clear long-term purpose, you can build capability and create a legacy that extends far beyond the event itself. Film has that same ability to bring people together and broaden representation. We are still at the beginning of that journey, but the direction is very clear.

articles.title: An MCU Favorite's Forgotten Marvel Return Happened Twelve Years Ago, Expanding Their Franchise Even More
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel One of the most fun aspects of the Marvel Cinematic Universe is seeing characters from one movie or TV series show up in another major project. This has been a consistent part of the franchise on the big screen since its inception in 2008. We all remember Hawkeye popping up in Thor, Black Widow's debut […]
articles.content:
The TV side of Marvel was unjustly overlooked by far too many fans, especially before the days of Disney+ originals like WandaVision and Loki . One of those underrated and underwatched series was Agent Carter , which put Peggy Carter at the forefront and showed us what she was up to after the events of Captain America: The First Avenger . With her impending return in Avengers: Doomsday , it's a good time to look back at her forgotten return, long before any of her latest film roles, in another undervalued series, Agents of SHIELD , which expanded the entire franchise in fun ways beyond the movies.

The events of Captain America: The First Avenger felt like a natural end for Peggy Carter. She was left behind in the past to live her life while we followed Steve as he was unfrozen in modern times. However, the Agent Carter One-Shot gave us a peek at what came next for her and then the success of that special spawned a TV series of the same name in 2015. The show gave us more of Hayley Atwell, had some intriguing storylines, and good spy action, yet not enough people watched it.

In between that One-Shot and the TV show, there was a forgotten Peggy appearance from 2014 that is one of her best. She popped up in the Season 2 premiere of Agents of SHIELD and had a recurring role through flashbacks. Her return in that premiere episode, titled “Shadows”, took us to 1945 and saw her work alongside the Howling Commandos as they arrested and interrogated Hydra agents and took hold of an important artifact known as the Obelisk. This set the stage for a crucial storyline about Inhumans and one of the show's main characters, Daisy Johnson.

For the fans who were invested in the MCU's shows, this felt like a big deal. It was a crossover spanning decades, gave us more of a beloved character, and even saw Peggy return later in the season in “The Things We Bury”. Unfortunately, this moment has been mostly forgotten by MCU fans. The franchise has kind of ignored Agents of SHIELD in general over the years, while Peggy has continued to return more than anyone expected. It's easy to forget about this 2014 appearance when she has shown up in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, What If…?, Avengers: Endgame , and more.

The TV side of things for the MCU wasn't all that established in 2014 when this crossover happened, which made it more special. It let the viewers know just how expansive this franchise could be. We had seen the movie characters show up in each other's projects but doing so on TV was totally different. Peggy Carter's appearance on Agents of SHIELD opened the door for her own series and allowed this show to explore the past. It also felt like a way to tie the films to the TV shows and truly sell the MCU's “it's all connected” gimmick.

The future of MCU television shows attempted to continue this trend. On Netflix, characters like Claire Temple appeared in everything from Daredevil to Luke Cage , before all the heroes on that streaming service came together for The Defenders . The stars of Cloak & Dagger popped up for an episode of The Runaways , which is the kind of thing that could only happen because of something like Peggy showing up in Agents of SHIELD .

Now, MCU TV shows do crossovers and cameos all the time. The Disney+ era for these series has been more pivotal to the larger franchise, with characters from the films appearing in Loki, WandaVision, The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, Ms. Marvel , and Hawkeye , among others. It has shown that the franchise is bigger than ever, which all goes back to that Agents of SHIELD appearance, which also set the tone for Peggy as a prominent figure. Not many people ever expected that, yet the character is bigger than ever today.

What are your thoughts on Peggy Carter's role in Agents of SHIELD ? Let us know in the comments.

articles.content:
Rob Lowe has said he asked to star in Ben Shapiro ‘s feature film " Confession " despite Shapiro considering him "way too handsome" for the part.

"I read the script, it was written by Ben Shapiro," Lowe said on the Second Thought podcast. "I called Ben and said, ‘This is fantastic.'"

Shapiro, who had met Lowe a couple of times in passing, had sent the script over in the hope the "West Wing" actor could suggest a leading man who wouldn't be "scared" to work with the conservative writer, who founded The Daily Wire website. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories NBCUniversal, Hornbill Capital Back EloElo, Parent of Indian Microdrama Platform Story TV, in $80 Million Funding Round Why 'Suits' Japan Swapped Drugs for Cash: NBCUniversal, TBS Format Chiefs on Localizing Hits at Taiwan Creative Content Fest

"And I go, ‘Yeah, me.' And he goes, ‘You're good with this?' I said, ‘I've worked with the most life-wring writers in the world. Why wouldn't I also work with the most right-wing writers in the world?'"

In a separate interview with writer Coleman Hughes, on his "Conversations With Coleman" podcast, Shapiro recounted a similar story, saying Lowe had been "really deeply affected by the script," which is set in Stalinist Russia and follows Lowe's character Alexi, an erstwhile literature professor who is interrogated by a former pupil turned KGB agent Vladimir (played by James Franco ) after he is accused of colluding with a dissident priest.

Shapiro said he told the star: "You're Rob Lowe. If you ask to play a part, the answer is yes, but I'm just telling you you're way too handsome for this."

Lowe admitted his reps hadn't been enthused by his decision to work with Shapiro, saying: "There were people who were definitely like, ‘Are you crazy?' But… I'm old enough, established enough, people know me well enough, to know that I'm not an ideologue at all. I'm not telling anybody how to live, how to think, on either side of the aisle. I've campaigned for Republicans. I've campaigned for Democrats…. I have my bona fides in both worlds." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The film, directed by Václav Marhoul ("The Painted Bird"), also stars Jennifer Jason Leigh, Nick Nolte, Emile Hirsch and Kodi Smit-McPhee. It is being distributed by the Daily Wire.

Lowe said the team had hoped for a traditional distributor or streamer to pick up the film but found every door closed. "It is challenging, it's a tough watch," he said of the subject matter. "But I see the movies that are celebrated out there. I see the movies that are picked for film — we got turned down by every single film festival. Summarily frog-marched out of any conversation. Now, this is a movie with me, Nick Nolte, James Franco, Emile Hirsch. I see what they're picking up. And it's all political."

"The thought would be, we'd play in a film festival, we would get some buzz — never happened — and then Netflix would pick it up… Crickets. Absolute crickets. So then it defaults to the Daily Wire to be the distributor. And I'm like, hell yeah. I want people to see this movie. And good for them for putting it out."

"But that wasn't originally going to be the life of the movie. My thought would be like, Focus Features would see it in Venice and like it. But people are definitely in a place where a lot of people cannot see a work just for its work. They have to do the math of ‘What does it mean?' and ‘What will people think?' and ‘Does that mean I'm on this side or does that mean I'm on that side?'"

He acknowledged that it was "the greatest irony" given the subject of the movie is about "wrongthink" in the Soviet Union, adding he has friends across the political spectrum. "For every Jane Fonda I have a Ben Shapiro. For every Jimmy Kimmel I've got Bill O'Reilly," Lowe said.

"I feel like that's what's lacking," he added. "People do not have any type of leash for other people in their orbit. But to me, that's what you want: people who think differently than you. And by the way, I'm not saying I agree with any of these people, but I don't want to hear the same conversation and the same story over and over. And I really appreciate different opinions."

articles.title: 4 Excellent Robert Pattinson Performances Outside of The Batman, Including His James Bond Audition
articles.summary: Yes, Bruce Wayne is the new James Bond. Movie fans around the world are still taking in the news that The Batman star Robert Pattinson has been cast in the lead role of the 26th film in the main James Bond franchise, reteaming Pattinson with director Denis Villeneuve. Pattinson is the first actor to play […]
articles.content:
The Devil All the Time (2020) Bond 26 will see Pattinson take on another of cinema’s most famous heroes, but he’s equally as skilled at playing bad guys, with his antagonistic role in this bleak Southern Gothic crime drama being his most viscerally disturbing. Based on Donald Ray Pollock’s novel of the same name, The Devil All the Time features a large ensemble of characters, though Arvin Russell (Tom Holland) is the central figure. An orphan living in 1960s West Virginia, Arvin is extremely protective of his adopted sister Lenora (Eliza Scanlen). When she is violated by reverend and sexual predator Preston Teagardin (Pattinson), Arvin seeks revenge, and is forced to go on the run after the ensuing confrontation. The Devil All the Time received mixed reviews upon release, though the performances of the cast, especially those of Holland and Pattinson were frequently praised. The latter’s depraved turn makes the viewer’s skin crawl, contrasting drastically against his more noble characters.

Even before the Bond casting, 2026 had already been a great year for Pattinson, as he’s appeared in three of the year's most acclaimed films, with his first collaboration with Villeneuve, the highly anticipated Dune: Part Three , still to come. Primetime is the only of the four films in which he’s played the lead role, namely that of real-life television reporter Chris Hansen, during an especially eventful and disastrous period in the production of Hansen’s famously controversial true crime series, To Catch a Predator . Hansen’s distinctively unusual public personas provide a strong basis off of which Pattinson constructs one of his boldest, most unpredictable performances. He consistently demonstrates the growing toll the horrific subject matter of his work takes on Hansen’s psyche, which collapses alongside the hit series as Hansen and his colleagues’ shared obsessions with both crime and punishment and personal fame tear them apart.

While Pattinson brought to life an all too realistic kind of evil with Preston Teagardin, he’s also highly dynamic as a more heightened villain in Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of Homer’s legendary heroic myth. One of the many suitors hoping to marry Penelope (Anne Hathaway) and claim the wealth of Ithaca’s missing king, Odysseus (Matt Damon), Antinous is the cowardly, manipulative opposite of The Odyssey ’s heroic lead, but Pattinson’s over the top portrayal of his conniving, backstabbing behavior makes it all darkly comical in the best of ways. The character is lying and performing so constantly that he seems to have convinced himself that he actually is the noble person he pretends to be and Pattinson makes his egocentrism equally pathetic and unnerving due to the wholehearted energy with which Antinous embraces his own illusion.

Pattinson’s first role in a Nolan film is the one that is itself basically an audition for Bond. A palindromic science fiction epic, Tenet ‘s unnamed protagonist (John David Washington) is a former CIA agent recruited into an even more secretive intelligence agency to neutralize a terror threat involving technology from the future that can alter one’s perception of time. Pattinson’s Neil is a jovial mercenary the Protagonist recruits as his partner, who proves both incredibly well-prepared for and enthusiastic about the bizarre mission.

The complexity of Tenet ’s sci-fi plot and certain other stylistic choices have made it one of Nolan’s most divisive films, though even many viewers with more negative opinions of it name the performances from Washington and Pattinson, and the dynamic between their characters, as undeniable strengths. Playing an espionage agent with his natural British accent is probably the most direct possible preparation Pattinson could do for Bond before actually getting the role and his scene stealing work in Tenet proved he could be a physically commanding hero while also portraying significant growth and nuance for a character within a blockbuster context. Neil seems to enjoy his work even more than most iterations of Bond do, but that just proves that Pattinson will be prepared for the more lighthearted and comedic aspects of the role , while Batman and many of his other characters make it plain that he also has the cold edge and dramatic capacity for when the spy work gets serious.

What are your favorite Robert Pattinson performances? Discuss in the comments.

Around this time one year ago, Hédi Zardi, head of the Marrakech Film Festival 's Atlas Programs, was approached by a young filmmaker with an urgent request. The director, who had a feature film in development at the industry event, was just putting the finishing touches on a short film. "She just asked, ‘Hedi, I would love to meet Venice,'" Zardi recalls.

As luck would have it, a key member of the Venice Film Festival programming team was also in attendance. Zardi connected the duo, who hit it off over a leisurely coffee. That ability to make an "easy connection" in Marrakech is by design, Zardi notes, with the industry team carefully curating its program to facilitate meetings of both the formal and informal variety. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Pixar Names Jonathan Garson as President; Jim Morris Moves to Emeritus Role

"Everything is possible," Zardi insists, with a wave-of-the-hand nonchalance that undersells the work he and his team do to achieve the best possible outcome for every film entrusted into their hands. It's a philosophy he describes as "curat[ing] each moment” and attempting — through a combination of one-on-one meetings, casual lunches and other events — to "build connections to see what happens."

For Shaden Safieddine Tazi — the young Moroccan Lebanese director who came to Zardi with her urgent appeal — that approach resulted in a trip to Venice, where her short "A Few Moments of Happiness" was selected for the festival's Horizons section, winning the award for best short film.

It's been just eight years since the Marrakech Film Festival introduced its industry program, Atlas Workshops , which was conceived as a springboard for filmmakers from Africa and the Arab world. (It's now one of several sections joined under the Atlas Programs banner.) This year's event runs Nov. 22 – 26. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Through a combination of mentorship programs, workshops and both one-on-one meetings and pitching sessions with industry professionals from around the world, the platform — which was founded by festival artistic director Rémi Bonhomme — was designed to boost directors who often face a dearth of exposure on the wider festival and industry circuit.

Eight years later, the event's track record speaks for itself: Since its first edition, 42 projects that have passed through the Atlas Workshops have been selected by Cannes, Venice or Berlin. Nearly half the films in this year's main competition in Marrakech are alumni of the program, including Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo's Cannes Caméra d'Or winner “Ben'Imana” (pictured above) and Rafiki Fariala's Un Certain Regard prizewinner “Congo Boy,” while the top prize at last year's festival, the Étoile d'Or, went to Erige Sehiri's migrant drama "Promised Sky,” a former Atlas participant.

That progression is indicative of a broader strategy crafted by Bonhomme and Zardi, who joined Atlas Workshops in 2023, to "offer support at the different stages of a film, from the development to the distribution," Zardi says.

That begins not only with the difficult selection process — this year saw 30 feature films in development, production or post-production chosen from 410 submissions — but with an insistence on keeping the event at what Zardi describes as a "human size."

"This boutique size allows people to mingle more easily than is possible in bigger markets or bigger industry events, where people need to be more efficient. Here, they allow themselves to spend time," he explains. "This quality time for work and networking is crucial. The idea of being too big might affect the quality of the event and what people are coming here to look for."

Festival programmers, he notes, have found Atlas' selection of pix-in-post to be fertile ground for the coming year's lineup, while the pared-down program means they "could also have time to meet projects in development to see what is coming up in two or three years." Similarly, the distributors and sales agents who typically make up the event's 200-strong contingent of industry guests can "discover the upcoming films without any pressure [and] allow themselves to be more curious." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Partly that owes to the event's curation, which is as rigorous with its guest list as its lineup. "We have to say no to a lot of people," Zardi admits. "We limit the access. It creates more excitement. It creates some buzz. And it's good for the projects," he adds. "This is a really safe environment that we have to protect, because it's the size that allows people to discover something that is not expected."

Thirty projects made the cut for this year's Atlas Workshops, with 11 of those currently in production or post-production and 14 in development. In addition, five projects have been selected for Atlas Close-Ups, a section devoted to emerging voices in Moroccan cinema.

The event boasts a loaded lineup, with new features from Palestinian filmmaker Laila Abbas ("Thank You for Banking With Us!"), Sudan's Amjad Abu Alala ("You Will Die at Twenty"), Morocco's Meryem Benm'Barek ("Behind the Palm Trees") and Moroccan French filmmakers Sofia Alaoui ("Animalia") and Yasmine Benkiran ("Queens") among the selection. Five first-time directors will also present their debut features, including Lebanon's Jessy Moussallem, whose short film "Faux Bijoux" premiered at Sundance, and Rwandan director Samuel Ishimwe, who won a Silver Bear in Berlin for his short film "Imfura."

"All these films are bringing me a different kind of cinema," Zardi says, pointing to the evolution of filmmaking in the region. "We are not only [seeing] classic, dramatic films from countries of the South that reflect something expected from international audiences. These directors now have a different professional dynamic to try new things and to surprise us," he continues. "I like the idea that, from this region, they are trying genre films; they relate national or regional history through intimate stories. It's not an expected, classic storytelling, which used to be the case."

That so many Arab and African filmmakers, such as Dusabejambo and Venice prizewinner Abu Alala, are enjoying breakout success on the festival circuit doesn't come as a surprise to Zardi, an industry veteran who co-founded the Paris-based sales and production company Luxbox a decade ago. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"There is a variety, and the market is reacting to this," he says. "If the region was offering the same thing each year, as a buyer, you can be bored. They want to [come to Marrakech] because they are aware that there are new things to discover."

Last year, the Marrakech team launched Atlas Distribution Meetings, which brings more than 60 key players in sales and distribution to the Moroccan event. From a practical perspective, this allows them — through both the festival selection and the industry program — to sample a wide variety of new and established talents from Africa and the Middle East.

It also fosters a rare opportunity "to encourage dialogue between the sales agents and the distributors from our region," Zardi says, while also putting them in the same room with their European counterparts.

"Distributors from MENA or Africa might not be key priorities for sales agents during the big markets, because they are facing other challenges. So the idea is to allow them to have this [opportunity] to meet with the distributors of our region," he says. "And the fact that distributors from the Arab world and Africa can also meet European distributors because they are doing the same job — not in the same reality, but it's very inspiring for them to share these ecosystems."

Last year, Marrakech rebranded its industry event, which is now organized under the Atlas Programs banner. That includes the flagship Altas Workshops section; Atlas Station, which provides 10 Moroccan directors or producers with support aimed at strengthening their skills and opening up their projects to international audiences; Atlas Distribution, which encourages the presentation of Moroccan, Arab and African films to new audiences in the region; and Atlas Press, which seeks to strengthen the culture of film criticism in Morocco.

The event's evolution, says Zardi, points to a commitment "to avoid having a single template that is called the Atlas Workshops that will repeat each year."

"After each Atlas Workshops, we coordinate, we do an evaluation, we see what works, what doesn't work," he says. "My idea is to never stop reshaping the editorial offer that we are bringing to the region…and to remain constantly aware of the changes." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

articles.title: Marshals Isn't The Only Taylor Sheridan Project With Thoughtful Things To Say About Missing Indigenous Women
articles.summary: It's important to tell these stories.
articles.content:
I’ve always had a major appreciation for Taylor Sheridan ’s shows, and the way many of them include prominent storylines about American Indians. Specifically, because I know there are so many stories about missing and murdered Indigenous women that we’ll never know, I really love it when one of his projects focuses on that topic. The Yellowstone spinoff Marshals has done it quite well. However, one of his early movies did too, and we need to talk about it.

As Marshals , which Sheridan is an EP on, has aired on the 2026 TV schedule , it’s made a point of including big stories and cases about the American Indians who live at Broken Rock. Specifically, in Season 1, Episode 5, “Lost Girls,” one of Tate’s friends, Hailey, goes missing. When it came out, Mo Brings Plenty, who plays Mo and is the show’s American Indian affairs coordinator , told me he thought the Yellowstone spinoff handled this problem “honestly.”

He also reiterated that this is a “real-life issue,” as women and men go missing often. It’s something he’s had to deal with in his own life too, as his nephew, Cole Brings Plenty, went missing and was found dead in 2024. Now, his story has become part of Marshals , as it inspired the case in Season 2, Episode 6 , which follows Mo and Kayce after they find out that his nephew has been killed.

These days, when Taylor Sheridan and his work get brought up, his shows, like Yellowstone and Landman , are typically what we’re talking about. However, before he was one of television's biggest writers and producers, his movies made quite the splash. In fact, Wind River is considered one of his best . It specifically focuses on a case involving an American Indian woman who is found dead in the middle of winter.

Overall, I found Wind River to be an incredibly moving film while also being peppered with the Taylor Sheridan writing and action his shows are known for. I also appreciated how it managed to be an entertaining thriller while also poignantly handling such an important and delicate topic.

articles.content:
Tudor Vladimir Panduru touched down at the ToruńCamerimage Film Festival in Poland last week where the cinematographer and frequent Cristian Mungiu collaborator reflected on how he crafted the visuals for the Romanian filmmaker's Palme d'Or winning title Fjord .

Panduru and Mungiu have been working together for more than a decade, working on titles such as Graduation and R.M.N. in addition to Fjord , and the DP notes that the long relationship means they have built a shorthand and "very specific visual language" together.

Mungiu is known for his very long takes – notably shooting a 17-minute shot in R.M.N. – and Panduru says the pair have "perfected the way we work with these long takes." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Festivals 'Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother' DP On Balancing Action Sequences With A Man's "Spiritual Journey And Struggles Of Trying To Step Up As A Father" -- ToruńCamerimage Festivals 'Fatherland' Takes Top Prize At ToruńCamerimage; 'Wild Horse Nine' Wins Audience Award

"We are comfortable with each other and we prepare a lot," he says. "He brought me in on this project quite early on in pre-production and then we went to Norway to scout for locations." Fjord , which is released by Neon in the U.S. and UK, follows a Norwegian woman (Renate Reinsve) and her devout Romanian husband (Sebastian Stan) who relocate with their five children to a remote, close-knit coastal town. Their teenage children form a fast bond with a neighboring family as unease begins to simmer around their rigid beliefs. When allegations of abuse emerge, they are forced to confront a system of judgement that blurs the line between concern and prejudice.

"Cristian is a good observer, and he always wants to be truthful," says Panduru. "And I follow that in that process of trying not to be judgemental in my approach as well.

He continues: "From the point of the script, the story had some specificity. The fact that these two families were close to each other meant that we had to find a place or a geography that would tell that from the start, and that was the hardest thing throughout the process of the scout."

The team scouted from Bergen to Ålesund before finding neighbouring houses overlooking the water for the main characters. "It wasn't so common to find two houses in such close vicinity because when we took the first photos and watched them, we were totally immersed in that universe. So, that's a layer that wasn't present in the script." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

He admits that scheduling and the remote location made it a "hard production" at times. "It was tricky organizing everything and getting to the locations. You had to either take two ferries or a long road and a ferry, so we were quite stuck there. It was really remote."

A further challenge, he notes, was the fact that the story takes place across three seasons but was only shot in March and April. "When we scouted the third time in January, there was a lot of snow and we were hoping to have images with small characters in the snow, but it wasn't like that. We had to use a bit of VFX on the way. The only evening shots that had a lot of snow were shot on the weekend because that's when it happened.

"Our first AD was the one who proposed we shoot when it was snowing at the weekend and we even convinced Sebastian to come with us for one of the shots. I think that was a really interesting part of doing Fjord , was the fact that the crew, who were from Romania, Norway, Finland, Sweden and all over, was really homogenous. We really were like a family, so we felt support from all sides."

Thanks to weather conditions, Panduru points out that one of the film's more emotional scenes when Reinsve's character's children are taken into custody, was actually shot on the first day of the shoot "because we were supposed to shoot in the snow."

"Shooting such an intense scene for the first day was really interesting but, in a way, because we did that at the beginning, everybody understood what the film was about," he says.

Panduru says that one of the most challenging sequences was the "jump in the water", a long take which sees the camera follow Reinsve's character searching on the ground to jumping into the sea.

"Because we shoot in these long takes, the most important thing was to have the emotional trajectory of the situation," he says. "We thought a lot about how to achieve that moment in a technical way, and we thought about cranes and drones, but it wasn't the right thing. I proposed to Cristian to test to see if I could physically jump in the water with them and we did it in a weekend and it worked."

articles.title: This Masters of the Universe Auction Is Proving Skeletor is More Popular Than He-Man
articles.summary: Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios This summer Masters of the Universe brought He-Man, Skeletor and the other heroes and villains of Eternia to cinemas in a way they have never been seen before. In a colorful, fantasy extravaganza directed by Travis Knight that did not shy away from depicting the characters of the 1980s cartoon series in all their glory, […]
articles.content:
It is usually frowned upon to root for the villain but Skeletor is the kind of bad guy that can easily get fans on side in wanting to see them win the day just one time. Thanks to this auction, it seems that Skeletor may finally get his victory. Among the many lots available, a complete Havok Staff is bidding at $3,250 and could sell for one of the highest prices in the entire auction. Listed as good in used condition, the staff measures a mighty 69 inches and was used by Leto in a scene when Beast Man has returned to Snake Mountain after failing to capture Adam and take the Power Sword. Meanwhile, the stunt prop Power Sword used by Galitzine's He-Man in several action sequences along with its sheath is selling for only $1,350. This version of the weapon is made of silver painted rubber so it could be used for fight sequences, but also features in a scene where several Eternians inspect it to check it is really the Power Sword. It looks like this is one showdown where good does not conquer evil.

Masters of the Universe took a long time to make it to the big screen, going through several iterations before finally landing at Amazon MGM Studios and gaining Knight as director. When the film opened earlier this year, the reviews from fans were mostly positive, but the film struggled to become the box office smash many believed it could be. The movie ended its theatrical run on a $114 million worldwide total, well below its reported $170-200 million budget. While many immediately labeled the movie a flop, this was only half the story as is the case with many releases now thanks to streaming. Arriving on Prime Video a short time later, Masters of the Universe became one of the biggest streaming movies of the year, spending several weeks at the top of the streamer's chart and redeeming its lacking box office result .

What became more impressive was the turnaround in opinions of the film and an unexpected regret from many who watched on streaming that they had not been able to see it on the big screen. In several subsequent interviews, Knight noted that Amazon MGM's main focus had always been on the film's streaming performance, so the lacking theatrical showing did not seem to bother them. Having said that, it has now been several months since the film's huge streaming debut but there has still been no confirmation of whether a sequel will be going ahead. The film's post-credits scenes set up the return of Skeletor as well as the arrival of She-Ra and Hordak, but whether fans will ever get to see that happen seems to still be in the hands of the studio.

Would you like to own a piece of Masters of the Universe ? Should the movie get a sequel? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.

"Chronicles From the Siege," a drama directed by Palestinian-Syrian filmmaker Abdallah Al-Khatib, has been pulled by its Algerian producer from the Marrakech Film Festival in protest against Morocco's diplomatic ties with Israel.

The film, which won the best first feature award at the Berlin Film Festival, was set to compete at Marrakech's 23rd edition, which kicks off Friday.
