According to the festival, Al-Khatib has strongly opposed the decision and made clear that he wants his film to screen in Marrakech.

"The Algerian producer justified the decision by referring to the recent announcement of Moroccan and Israeli cooperation," the festival said. "This is the producer's own position, on the basis of which they decided to withdraw the film, despite having initially approved its selection and despite the clear opposition expressed by the film's Palestinian-Syrian director and the entire Palestinian cast and crew."

Morocco normalized relations with Israel in 2020 as part of the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords. The two countries have since expanded their cooperation.

The withdrawal comes despite the producers having formally approved the film's selection on June 1.

Variety has reached out to Salah Issaad of Issaad Film Productions for comment. The film's other lead producer is Taqiyeddine Issaad.

The decision is particularly notable given the film's history with Marrakech. In 2024, "Chronicles From the Siege" received support from the festival's Atlas Workshops, a talent development program for filmmakers and producers from Morocco, the Arab world and Africa, and won its Atlas Prize for post-production.

The film subsequently premiered in Berlin's Perspectives section, where it won the best first feature award.

Despite the director's objections, the Marrakech Film Festival said it had no choice but to respect the rights holder's decision. "While the festival acknowledges the director's expressed wish to present his film in Marrakech, it is bound to respect the decision of the company holding the film's rights and is therefore unable to retain it in the festival's program," the festival said.

Inspired by Al-Khatib's personal experience during the siege of Yarmouk Camp in Syria, "Chronicles From the Siege" follows several Palestinians struggling to survive amid hunger, isolation and violence. According to the film's sales notes, it reflects the broader Palestinian experience of siege, from the Nakba to the present day.

The film interweaves stories of friendship, intimacy and survival, exploring how life under siege transforms even the simplest human experiences into struggles for survival.

articles.content:
With GTA 6 sitting at a 99/100 aggregate review score on the website Metacritic , it sits among the highest-reviewed games of the year. At the time of writing, this average is based on reviews from 98 different critics across PlayStation 5 and Xbox, excluding PC and Nintendo Switch 2, as GTA 6 is not available on these platforms. It is clear that GTA 6 is a special game and will likely see massive sales even with the decision to exclude physical versions. Rockstar Games has clearly created a generational game.

With reviews for Grand Theft Auto 6 finally going live, its 99 score shouldn't come as a surprise. This makes it one of the best-reviewed games of 2026, something that comes after its Game of the Year nomination . Many were surprised to see a game that had not yet been released, let alone had reviews published, be chosen for this short list, but its Metacritic score justifies its placement there.

Not only that, but the official voice actress for Lucia has been revealed as Manni L. Perez thanks to her nomination for Best Performance at The Game Awards. This information has been one of the most highly debated topics surrounding the game. Though fans still do not know the credits for Jason, Perez's confirmation gives fans yet another idea of what to expect from GTA 6 .

It remains to be seen if GTA 6 will win GOTY at The Game Awards this year, but Rockstar Games can be proud of the product they released if the review score is anything to go by. For comparison, Grand Theft Auto 5 currently sits at a 97 on Metacritic, showing the series' legacy. Reviews are still early for GTA 6, and we may see its score shift throughout the week as more reviews come in.

As for the game itself, GTA 6 is set to launch on November 19th , ending the legendary lead-up to its release. Fans don't have long before they can return to Vice City and experience one of the biggest games in the history of the industry. articles.title: Marrakech Film Festival Grows Its Awards-Season Clout With 'Artificial,' 'The Debut,' 'Fjord' and Other Oscar Hopefuls
articles.summary: It’s roughly six thousand miles as the falcon flies from Hollywood’s Dolby Theatre to the Palais des Congrès, which will play host to more than a dozen gala screenings and world premieres at the 23rd edition of the Marrakech Film Festival, taking place Nov. 20 – 28. But for many of the Oscar hopefuls looking […]
articles.content:
It's roughly six thousand miles as the falcon flies from Hollywood's Dolby Theatre to the Palais des Congrès, which will play host to more than a dozen gala screenings and world premieres at the 23rd edition of the Marrakech Film Festival , taking place Nov. 20 – 28.

But for many of the Oscar hopefuls looking to jumpstart their campaigns during the furious, four-month home stretch before the Academy Awards, the Moroccan festival has become as much an award-season fixture as FYC screenings at the Egyptian Theatre or whistle-stop tours of luncheons scattered throughout the Hollywood Hills. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Canelo Alvarez vs. Christian M'billi on DAZN: Here’s How to Watch the WBC Title Boxing Match Live Online Here's Where to Get a Sony PlayStation 5 Pro Online, Ahead of the 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Release

Credit Rémi Bonhomme, now in his sixth year as artistic director, for mapping out a "strategic vision" that plants the Marrakech Film Festival squarely on the award-season circuit. "Being at the end of the year, at the beginning of the Oscar campaign, Marrakech has really become one of the important stops," Bonhomme says. Hollywood tastemakers agree, with AMPAS CEO Bill Kramer among those who made the trip last year, underscoring the festival's importance at a time when foreign members are becoming an increasingly influential voting body within the Academy.

This year's event opens with " The Debut ," Jesse Eisenberg's community-theater comedy, backed by A24, which stars best actress frontrunner Julianne Moore. Meanwhile, " Artificial ," Luca Guadagnino's buzzy Sam Altman biopic, starring Andrew Garfield, and "Paper Tiger," director James Gray's crime drama starring Miles Teller, Scarlett Johansson and Adam Driver, will be feted with gala screenings in Marrakech as they vie for coveted Oscar nods. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

There's also a robust contingent of films that will be representing their countries in the best international feature race, with 11 such titles tapped for this year's lineup, among them Romanian auteur Cristian Mungiu's Cannes-winning social drama "Fjord," starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, and Rwandan debutante Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo's Cannes Camera d'Or winner "Ben'Imana."

That so many Oscar contenders are playing in Marrakech speaks not only to its strategic placement on the calendar, but to a carefully considered approach to its scale — what Bonhomme describes as the festival's "human size" — that affords maximum exposure for all the films on offer.

"The question of the visibility the festival gives to films is very important, and for me, it's at the heart of the work I'm doing — both for those films campaigning for the Oscars , but also for the first and second films of the competition," Bonhomme explains. "We really support them in a very tailor-made way, because those films will be seen by the whole delegation of distributors that we invite. Distributors come to Marrakech with not so many films to watch, so they have real attention to give to these films."

That fact gets to the heart of what he describes as "the spirit of the festival," which in its curation puts an emphasis on "being tailor-made” and ensuring “people have time to meet."

"Marrakech is a place of encounters — between artists, between artists and the audience," he says. "We're not a market. I don't use the word market. It's meetings, workshops — which makes a big difference. Because people are not overwhelmed with too many meetings, too many people." It's precisely why he believes "the amazing artists that we gather every year come back."

While other events in the region offer a dedicated platform for African and Arab filmmakers, few, if any, manage to also attract quite such a dazzling constellation of Hollywood and international luminaries, with jury president Marion Cotillard, Oscar hopeful Guadagnino and screen icons John Turturro and Jeff Goldblum — the focus of a special tribute — all walking the red carpet this year. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"We are a festival where the artists we invite have time — they have time to meet with each other, which is not really often, especially when we speak about the biggest figures we invite every year," says Bonhomme. "This idea, the human-scale vision of the festival, is both for the audience, for the younger filmmakers, for the people from the industry, but also for all the big names that are coming and coming back to the festival."

Take the French screen star Cotillard, who Bonhomme calls "a very close friend of the festival since the very beginning," or Guadagnino and Gray, both of whom have served as jury president in previous editions. They'll be taking part in the festival's Conversations series alongside two-time Palme d'Or winner Cristian Mungiu ("Fjord"), who last year served as the patron of the Atlas Workshops. This year that honor will go to Brazilian auteur Kleber Mendonça Filho, who in the midst of his 2025 Oscar campaign for "The Secret Agent" also made a pit stop in Marrakech.

"We managed to create a very special place and open a real dialogue that's quite unique between established filmmakers and emerging talents," Bonhomme says. "I think this possibility of both accompanying emerging voices while also creating this bridge with the biggest names in world cinema…makes Marrakech a very, very special and unique space."

Joining Cotillard on this year's jury are Danish actor Claes Bang ("The Square"); Luxembourg actor Vickey Krieps ("Corsage"); French British actor Emma Mackey ("Sex Education"); French actor and director Gilles Lellouche ("Beating Hearts"); Tunisian director Kaouther Ben Hania ("The Voice of Hind Rajab"); British filmmaker Andrew Haigh ("All of Us Strangers"); French Senegalese filmmaker Ramata-Toulaye Sy ("Banel & Adama"); and Moroccan director and producer Saïd Hamich Benlarbi ("Across the Sea").

They'll be awarding the festival's top prize, the Étoile d'Or, to one of the 14 features from first- and second-time directors playing in the main competition. Among them are a trio of world premieres. "Alkebulan," by Moroccan director Yassine Marco Marroccu, is an adventure film set in the Sahara in the 1960s and Italy in the 1930s. Iranian Norwegian filmmaker Farzad Samsami, meanwhile, arrives with "Waves of Silence," a moral drama about migrant shipwrecks, shot in Morocco and starring Amine Ennaji. Finally, "Cairo Shadows" is an intimate thriller from directors Rani and Salem Massalha that's set in the Coptic Christian community in Egypt. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Alongside "Artificial" and "Paper Tiger," the festival's gala screenings strand will present Noah Segan's "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York," with lead actor Turturro in attendance, and Laïla Marrakchi's "Strawberries," which will represent Morocco in the international feature Oscar race. The section also includes two world premieres: Brazilian director Fellipe Barbosa's "Leila and the Night," inspired by the life of Moroccan photographer Leila Alaoui and starring Roschdy Zem and Marina Foïs; and Egyptian filmmaker Omar Hilal's "His Weakest Creatures," which pairs Egyptian stars Ahmed Helmy and Hend Sabry together on screen for the first time.

The host nation, meanwhile, is well represented, with 11 films playing across its various sections. Describing it as "a good year for Moroccan films," Bonhomme also points to a trio of movies shot in the North African country — Barbosa's "Leila and the Night"; Samsami's "Waves of Silence"; and "The Roses of Marrakesh," by Italian filmmaker Ginevra Elkann — as evidence that “we have more and more international filmmakers coming to shoot in Morocco."

This year's event included two last-minute additions that were set to premiere at Saudi Arabia's Red Sea Film Festival, whose 2026 edition was cancelled after an escalation in the conflict between the Kingdom and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels, who targeted several Saudi cities.

Bonhomme says the Marrakech fest already "expressed our solidarity with the team of Red Sea," adding, "It's always very sad news when a festival has to cancel." While stressing that Morocco is far removed from the Iran conflict and the ongoing war in Gaza, he notes that "festivals are alive, so festivals are always reflecting what's happening in the world, especially in this region."

"We welcome at the festival lots of filmmakers coming from countries that are directly affected by the war [in Gaza]. We also welcome films that deal directly with the current war," he says. "We also are in North Africa, which is a region that is also very protected from what's happening in the Middle East. So we have the possibility in Marrakech to still be a safe place where we can give a certain resonance of what's happening there."

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI Is One of Gaming's Greatest Achievements (Review)
articles.summary: I've spent weeks driving, flying, boating, and parachuting my way across Leonida in Grand Theft Auto VI, and I'm just as awestruck by what Rockstar Games has crafted now as I was when I first began playing. GTA VI features what is almost certainly the most impressive world ever created in a video game, boasting […]
articles.content:
When combined with its strong protagonists, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, and a compelling central narrative, these strides make Grand Theft Auto VI not only a monumental step forward for the Grand Theft Auto franchise, but for gaming as a whole. With GTA VI , Rockstar has made what is unquestionably the defining game of this console generation and has yet again established what is possible in the AAA space.

It should come as no surprise that Grand Theft Auto VI is Rockstar's largest game to date , but what I remain astounded by is the level of density to its world. Yes, there are more highways and back alleys that you can race through than ever as you try to avoid the police after robbing a nearby pawn shop, but it's the interior locations of GTA VI that I've been left baffled by.

While not every building within Grand Theft Auto VI is able to be freely explored, there are hundreds of them that you can sleuth around. Every bank, liquor store, and thrift shop feels completely unique unto itself, with plenty of other houses and other buildings being left open for you to enter at any point. Occasionally, the game will call your attention toward some of these locations with specialized events, but others I randomly stumbled upon in my time playing only to find rare collectibles or stashes of money.

This attention to detail is also true of GTA VI's various regions, of which there are countless. Each area of Leonida feels like a distinct universe of its own that's easy to get lost within for hours on end. Vice City might seem like the main hub within GTA VI , which it is to some degree, but navigating through dilapidated slums or backwoods mountainous locations can often be just as thrilling, albeit for completely different reasons.

Even after having put a good 50 to 60 hours into Grand Theft Auto VI , there are sections of the map that I've come nowhere close to uncovering. The game's main missions do their best to give you a taste of everything its world has to offer, from the skyscrapers of Vice City to the grimy swamps of southern Leonida, but even then, there are far-off locations that you'll never find unless you intentionally go out of your way to do so.

It's this constant push to explore Leonida that makes Grand Theft Auto VI so compelling. Even if you don't have a certain mission or activity to do in a given area, there's always the possibility that you'll run into a dynamic world event that could tell a smaller story that's just as exciting as what you'll find in the game's main missions.

Generally speaking, Grand Theft Auto VI is quite similar from a gameplay perspective to past entries. However, Rockstar has incorporated much of the realism that was seen in Red Dead Redemption 2 with GTA VI , which leads to some sizable alterations that the series has yet to see. No longer do you have an endless arsenal of weapons to pull out of thin air, as Jason and Lucia can only carry a maximum of two longarms at once. Similar limitations are put on the amount of stolen goods that you can pick up, the space in your car's trunk, or the types of vehicles that you're capable of hijacking.

These changes, while they might seem simple, completely reshape your approach to just about every scenario in Grand Theft Auto VI . Heists take far more planning, as you can't simply bust into a high-security bank with ammo strapped to Jason and/or Lucia like Rambo and plan to take out any cops that might come after you. You'll often have to choose the right weapon, car, and escape route for a situation long before you've ever started to execute a robbery.

In addition, police are far more difficult to evade, as they'll patrol areas where you've committed crimes long after you've left the area. This leads to the cat-and-mouse game of cops vs. robbers being far more engaging than anything else seen in the Grand Theft Auto series.

These adjustments to many of the core systems in GTA VI help really deepen the player's connection to Jason and Lucia and their struggle. No longer do you feel like a one-man army that can take on anything the police and military might throw at you, but instead, a small-time criminal who is just trying to find a way to skip town and stay alive. Although some might enjoy the power fantasy elements of GTA, they're still readily present in Grand Theft Auto VI in spite of Rockstar dialing things back just a bit.

Grand Theft Auto VI also does a phenomenal job of making you feel broke, as there is a greater emphasis on money in this installment than any one before it. While money had some rather limited uses in past games, GTA VI requires you to spend your hard-earned money on everything from fast travel to upgrading your car's specs. This, in turn, leads to you planning your next big score more often, as the need for cash necessitates just about everything that you can do. The only downside on this front is that it can often be annoying to fence some of the cash, drugs, or other stolen goods that you'll get your hands on, as those who buy these items are a bit too few and far between.

Grand Theft Auto VI's narrative is perhaps the thing that Rockstar has kept hidden the most prior to the game's release. This decision is one that I ended up being thrilled by, as there are numerous surprises tied to Jason and Lucia's story, even in its earliest moments. To that end, there's not a lot that I want to say about GTA VI's story myself, other than the fact that I was enthralled with it from start to finish.

Perhaps my only issue with the central story of GTA VI is just tied to its pacing. With the game boasting around 100 missions in total, there are definitely some stretches toward the middle of the story where it feels like the throughline narrative is put on the back burner for a bit too long. While there are still plenty of great sequences that happen during these narrative lulls, I often found myself wanting to more quickly get back to the story's main hook.

As far as character development goes, Jason and Lucia are the stars of GTA VI and immediately become some of the best protagonists in Grand Theft Auto's storied history. Seeing how each navigates their own personal turmoil while also relying on the other for support represents some of Rockstar's best writing in the entirety of GTA VI . In fact, I only wish Rockstar dug a bit deeper into some of the backstories and trauma that Jason and Lucia carry with them. Not doing so makes each feel like they're being at a distance from the player a bit too much.

Outside of Jason and Lucia, there are also plenty of side characters that the pair come into contact with over the course of Grand Theft Auto VI . Some of these characters, like the strategic bank robber Raul or Cal, Jason's hyperactive best friend, ended up being some of my favorites in the entirety of the game. Others, however, end up being far more forgettable and have their own mission lines that end up being some of the most boring in GTA VI .

On the whole, Rockstar's writing in Grand Theft Auto VI is incredibly strong. This is particularly true when it comes to its humor, as there are a multitude of radio shows, podcasts, and characters in the game that made me audibly laugh on numerous occasions. There were even long stretches of playtime where I'd do nothing but sit on my in-game couch and watch TV just to see what kind of insanity Rockstar had cooked up. Even though some members of Rockstar's writing team didn't return for GTA VI , it truly feels like the studio hasn't skipped a bit with its satirical take on America.

Arguably where Grand Theft Auto VI takes its biggest leap forward, other than with its world design, is with its missions. While some of the main missions in GTA's past have been notoriously maligned (looking at you, crane mission from GTA V ), GTA VI packs far more of a punch on this front than ever before. By far the most stunning and exciting missions in the franchise are found within GTA VI , with some still leaving me speechless weeks after having finished them.

Obviously, not every mission in Grand Theft Auto VI ends up being a thrill ride, as there are some that rely a bit too heavily on simply driving from point A to B, or tailing targets before engaging in basic shootouts. Still, on average, there have been major improvements to GTA VI that have been made, with the game's high points being the highest in the entire series.

This is also true of the dozens of side activities that you can take part in at any point across Leonida. If you want to lose your life by hunting rare wildlife across the forests and hills, you can easily spend tens of hours doing this alone while netting yourself some big bucks. Scuba diving for treasure, mud racing, and getting in a quick round of mini-golf are just a handful of the dozens of things you can do in the game in between committing heists or taking on local gangs. Not all of it might be equally enjoyable to every player, but the sheer amount of side content that is included ensures that you'll easily be able to find something to do in your spare time.

To really put all of the main and side missions in GTA VI over the top is the game's music. Both the licensed soundtrack and the original score of GTA VI are excellent, with the score, in particular, being one of the best that I've heard in a game in a very long time. Not only does it offer a fantastic amount of variety in terms of genre, but its placement within these missions only heightens the stress or magnitude of key moments. Music has always been a key part of Grand Theft Auto, but like so many other aspects of this game, Rockstar has found a way to make its inclusion even better than before.

In every regard, Grand Theft Auto VI is an extraordinary achievement for Rockstar Games. Even with incredibly high expectations coming in, Rockstar found a way to surpass just about everything that I had hoped to see in GTA VI . The final product is one that I'm still spellbound by, as I struggle to understand how the studio was even capable of making such an engrossing and complex experience. Grand Theft Auto VI is unquestionably going to go down as a landmark release in gaming's history and will continue to consume both my thoughts and free time well into the future.

An advance copy of Grand Theft Auto VI on PS5 was provided by the developer for the purpose of this review.

articles.title: 4 Lesser-Known Sci-Fi Movies That Scored Over 90% With Audiences on Rotten Tomatoes
articles.summary: Unfortunately, not every good movie becomes popular, and there are many reasons why that happens. But when it comes to sci-fi, that's a bit of a shame, given how much the genre has to offer and how interesting it could be to see these stories reach a wider audience. Maybe you've come across some movies […]
articles.content:
If you're looking for something different to watch in the genre , especially movies that have won over quite a few viewers, we've put together 4 picks you might end up loving. They offer something for different tastes, but there's bound to be at least one that catches your interest.

Anyone who watched the iconic Firefly , which is now set to rise from the ashes with its revival , probably knows Serenity . But for the most part, it's not the kind of movie that immediately comes to mind when people talk about sci-fi. Still, its excellent audience score shows just how much potential this universe has left to explore . Serving as a continuation of the show, it follows Malcolm Reynolds (Nathan Fillion) and his crew, who make a living taking on small jobs aboard the Serenity until they find themselves caught up in a conspiracy. But their situation changes when they have to protect River Tam (Summer Glau), a young woman with special abilities who's being hunted by the government and may hold information that could put the entire Alliance at risk.

We get space chases, political intrigue, and confrontations with dangerous creatures. Even so, the movie's greatest asset is still the chemistry between the characters, which is one of the main reasons the original series became a cult classic . Even as the story grows in scale, Serenity remains focused on its crew and the relationships between its members. It also makes great use of its blend of sci-fi and Western elements without feeling like it's trying to imitate another franchise or filmmaking style. And for anyone who has never watched the original production, the movie is still worth checking out, as it does a great job of providing enough context to follow the story. Overall, it has plenty to offer fans while being accessible to newcomers, all without losing its own identity. It's also a pretty great comfort movie, honestly.

The biggest reason The Assessment is worth watching is that it's a dystopian film that doesn't feel all that far removed from reality, which makes everything both intriguing and unsettling. It starts with a question: what if people needed government approval to have children? In this story, we follow Mia (Elizabeth Olsen) and Aaryan (Himesh Patel), a couple living in a society where limited resources have led to strict regulations on reproduction. When they decide to have a child, they must undergo an assessment conducted by Virginia (Alicia Vikander), who moves into their home for some days to observe their behavior and determine whether they're fit to become parents. They go through a series of tests, but the whole experience is completely messed up.

You know those films that make you uncomfortable , but that's exactly what makes them so good? That's the case here, especially as Virginia starts crossing boundaries and putting the couple's relationship under pressure. The Assessment is not your typical movie about an authoritarian government because its central conflict is much more personal — the focus is on the characters confronting their choices, insecurities, and the way they see their own dynamic. Plus, the performances are outstanding, and you'll find yourself curious from the beginning about what's going to happen next. It's the kind of narrative that makes you think about life and family, and one that stays with you .

Here's a sci-fi that most people have probably never heard of, partly because it's a French production that uses the genre to explore a very specific plot. But just to give an idea of what to expect, one of its directors is Jean-Pierre Jeunet, the same one behind the beloved Amélie . Delicatessen takes us to a post-apocalyptic world where society has been so affected by food shortages that human flesh has become an alternative for survival. But things get crazier because most of the story happens inside a single apartment building, where Clapet (Jean-Claude Dreyfus), the owner of a butcher shop, is also responsible for hiring people to do odd jobs. The catch is that these employees tend to disappear, since the butcher turns them into the product of his establishment.

Despite its macabre premise, this isn't the kind of sci-fi movie that tries to terrify you . Instead, it leans into dark comedy, with touches of romance and, of course, suspense. The idea is to use the characters' behavior to show just how far people can go when survival is their only concern. As a result, Delicatessen gives us eccentric figures, insane situations, and humor that comes out of moments that would be absolutely horrifying in any other context. Basically, it's a film you finish watching and immediately describe as an experience in itself. It's also great to see a story that moves away from the usual end-of-the-world formula to explore something that's really a study of human nature.

This is where we get to look at the Marvel Cinematic Universe and DC Universe movies from recent years and have a little laugh , because Shin Ultraman is considered one of the best superhero movies by many people. This Japanese production reimagines the title character, who first appeared on TV back in the '60s , without getting rid of the elements that made him an icon. The story takes place in a world threatened by giant creatures known as S-Class Species and follows a specialized team tasked with fighting these monsters. However, a mysterious alien arrives on Earth and starts taking them on, eventually assuming a humanoid form and becoming known as Ultraman. So a few questions come up: does he really intend to protect humanity, or does he have something else in mind?

It's great to see a movie in this genre (even if it's also sci-fi) that actually has something to say, and that's a big part of what makes Shin Ultraman stand out. While the monster fights are one of the best parts, the film is also interested in how humans react when faced with something they can't understand or control. This opens the door to plenty of discussion about power, relationships between different species, and humanity's place when confronted with beings more advanced. At the same time, like Serenity , it doesn't forget its roots and holds on to much of the charm of the original show. It's also a pretty cool watch for Godzilla fans, especially those who enjoyed Shin Godzilla , since both share some similarities and references.

The European Film Academy will honor multi-award-winning Belgian directorial duo Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne with a Lifetime Achievement Award at its 39th European Film Awards in January 2027.

Among the most internationally acclaimed filmmakers to emerge from Belgium and Europe, the brothers have left an indelible mark on European cinema history over the past four decades with their films exploring what it means to live in a society shaped by inequality, migration, and economic pressure.

They founded their production company Les Films du Fleuve in 1987. Its early production including The Promise (1996) gave a taste of the distinctive cinematic approach steeped in social issues and authenticity.

Set in the industrial world of Liège, it followed Igor, a teenage mechanic's apprentice whose father is involved in the exploitation of undocumented workers.

Three years later, they would break out internationally with Rosetta , which won the brothers their first Cannes Palme d'Or.

In 2019, the Dardennes received the Cannes Best Director Award for Young Ahmed , while T ori and Lokita , a drama about two young migrants from Africa who have arrived in Belgium alone, received the the festival's 75th Anniversary Prize in 2022.

They were back at the festival in 2025 with Young Mothers , which received the Best Screenplay Award and the Ecumenical Jury Prize.

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda Movie Has One Challenge That Other Video Game Adaptations Never Faced
articles.summary: Mario talks. Sonic talks. Even the most stoic video game heroes usually have something to say when the situation gets desperate. Link, meanwhile, has spent nearly 40 years letting everybody else do the talking. He's saved Hyrule from destruction, fought some truly ridiculous monsters, and somehow managed to become one of Nintendo's most recognizable characters […]
articles.content:
The problem isn't that Link needs to deliver a bunch of witty one-liners. Please don't give him those. The appeal of the character has always been tied to the player's relationship with him. When you're playing Zelda , Link's reactions become your reactions. His decisions are yours to make, and even his personality leaves plenty of room for interpretation. A movie doesn't have that luxury. We won't be holding a controller or deciding whether Link should explore another cave before saving the kingdom. We'll be watching somebody else's version of him. Nintendo needs to make that version feel like Link without losing what made him special in the first place.

There's a reason Nintendo has kept Link relatively quiet throughout the series. He's not supposed to dominate conversations or explain every thought running through his head. He's the character players inhabit. When somebody asks him a question, the games generally let us imagine his response. That arrangement has worked for decades, but it creates an unusual problem when you take him out of the interactive world. Consider Ocarina of Time . Link spends the entire adventure surrounded by characters with strong personalities, from the endlessly talkative Navi to the mysterious Sheik. Yet he remains largely an observer. His expressions and actions tell us what we need to know because we're the ones making his choices. Even Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom maintain that approach while offering more insight into his relationships through Zelda's memories and diary entries. We learn that he's dependable, courageous, and occasionally rather difficult to understand. There's a person there. Nintendo just doesn't usually let him explain himself.

That's a tricky thing to translate into a movie. A completely silent Link might sound faithful to the games, but there's a difference between spending 40 hours controlling a character and spending two hours watching him. An actor needs something to work with, and the audience needs a reason to care about what happens to him beyond the fact that he's wearing the famous green tunic. I don't want Link turned into another generic action hero who cracks jokes whenever a monster appears. That would miss the point entirely. But giving him a recognizable personality doesn't mean abandoning his quiet nature. Think about how much an actor can communicate through frustration, curiosity, or even an awkward attempt to connect with somebody. Link doesn't need to become particularly talkative. He just needs to feel like a young man rather than a convenient pair of hands for the audience.

The other problem is that The Legend of Zelda has never been particularly interested in telling one definitive version of Link's story. He's been a farm boy, a young adventurer, a sailor, and a knight-in-training. Sometimes he's a child facing an enormous threat. Other times he's a young man dealing with responsibilities that nobody his age should have to carry. The games change their settings and timelines, but the basic idea remains remarkably consistent. An ordinary person finds himself caught up in something extraordinary. That's a perfectly good foundation for a movie, although the filmmakers will need to decide which parts of Link's personality carry across those different incarnations. His courage is obvious. His relationship with Zelda is another matter. The two have shared some wonderful moments throughout the series, but their dynamic changes considerably depending on the game. Breath of the Wild arguably offers the richest material for exploring that relationship because Zelda's memories reveal how much pressure both characters carry. There's a story there that doesn't require Link to spend half the movie explaining his feelings.

I'd actually be more concerned about the filmmakers making Link too familiar. Video game movies have a habit of giving their protagonists conventional personalities because somebody assumes audiences need constant dialogue and jokes to stay interested. But Link has survived this long precisely because Nintendo never treated him like every other adventure hero. His silence gives the player room to connect with him. The movie needs to find a cinematic equivalent for that relationship. Maybe he'll speak occasionally. Maybe he'll communicate more through expressions and actions. Either way, the important thing is that we understand what drives him and why protecting Hyrule matters to him. The Master Sword, the Triforce, and all those familiar locations will help sell the fantasy. Getting audiences invested in the person carrying that sword is a much harder assignment. Nintendo has spent decades letting players decide who Link is. Now the movie has to make that decision itself.

articles.title: 'Hazara Town' Review: A Restrained but Deeply Affecting Doc Portrait of an Afghan Refugee Family Living in Limbo
articles.summary: A gauze of dust covers everything in the Pakistani desert city of Quetta, rendering just about everything the same shade of bleached, parched beige — an in-between color for an in-between place, where many residents await change with no clear timeline. In the city quarter of Hazara Town, named for over half a million residents […]
articles.content:
A gauze of dust covers everything in the Pakistani desert city of Quetta, rendering just about everything the same shade of bleached, parched beige — an in-between color for an in-between place, where many residents await change with no clear timeline. In the city quarter of Hazara Town , named for over half a million residents from the ethnic Hazara community, displaced refugees from Afghanistan live in indefinite limbo: violently imperiled in their current sanctuary, but not yet granted asylum anywhere else. It's a despairing holding pattern through which everyday life, with its more modest domestic challenges and occasional joys, nonetheless continues: Khadim Dai ‘s patiently observed, intensely moving documentary “Hazara Town” sharply chronicles that simultaneous stasis and progress. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Microsoft Apologizes for Massive Outlook Outage, Affected Customers Can Request Credits for Service Interruption Microsoft Says 'No Evidence of Malicious Activity' in Global Outage of Outlook and Exchange Email as It Begins to Restore Services

The first feature-length film by the Afghan-born, Los Angeles-based Dai is a family affair, centered on the director's own stranded relatives: his sister-in-law, Sedeqa; his two young nieces, Machid and Mitra; and their doting grandparents. All are stranded in Quetta since fleeing Afghanistan, while Dai's brother Hussain has forged ahead, laying the groundwork for a new life in Canada. Following him is no simple matter, however. The asylum application process is slow and selective, and whole chapters of family life pass by as they wait to be reunited: Preteen Mitra, in particular, doesn't remember much of her father's presence at home, and communication by phone and video only partially bridges the gap.

Returning to Pakistan several years after his own departure, Dai embeds himself in the household, his camera capturing both the intimate daily routines of a splintered family — in particular, the growth of two girls around their father's absence — and wider currents of fear and sorrow in the Hazara community, where people increasingly find themselves as unsafe from ethnic and religious persecution as they were in the homeland they fled. Targeted killings are disturbingly commonplace, the rising death toll sporadically flashing on the screen with no further commentary. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Dai's camera records no violence, but instead spends much time in the local cemetery where the dead are buried with little ceremony — their portraits displayed for a time as a memorial before they, too, vanish. Deft, detailed sound design balances the lonely reverberations of the desert wind against the industrious tap-tap-tapping of local stonemasons at work on various grave markers: At least some in this stymied community have much to do. But the cemetery isn't presented only as a place of grief: It's also a gathering spot for people otherwise granted little social space, and in some of the film's most poignant tableaux, children chatter and play amidst these humble resting places.

Home, though, remains the most secure of spaces in an otherwise stateless existence: With its modest interior courtyard and few windows to the outside world, Dai's family's residence feels significantly turned inward. Though Machid and Mitra both go to school, classroom freedoms are curbed as Pakistan hands over responsibility for refugee education to the Taliban; it's within cramped domestic walls that the girls assert their evolving personalities and interests, rapidly maturing before our eyes.

Machid, a studious bookworm with a love of Judy Blume, dreams of richer education opportunities in the United States, while the rest of the family pins their hopes on Canada — sold to them via effortfully cheerful video missives from Hussain, marveling at differences in culture and weather. Good news does arrive from North America, but not for everyone, and so the family is further fragmented. Dai films each individual flight from the back window of the departing taxi, splashed with a bucket of water for good luck, the drips distorting one last look at those left behind in the rearview.

Also an accomplished cinematographer, Dai shoots these individually unremarkable episodes of daily survival — and occasional celebration — with a grace and sensitivity that cumulatively builds to something more than just diaristic in effect: “Hazara Town” is a quietly emphatic statement of presence for lives all too easily disappeared, or dismissed as statistics. And while it provides no tidy resolution to this collective narrative, there's at least a temporary, heart-filling interlude of reunion, before life pulls in a multitude of directions: For the refugee family, there's as much anguish in movement as in stillness, but a shred of hope too.

articles.title: ‘NAZA’ Team Sticking To Plan To Release Shattering Documentary On The Guardian Website Within Weeks — IDFA

But if co-directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor had prevailed, it might have gone straight from its Venice Film Festival premiere to The Guardian website. “At first me and Rachel thought, let's put it out online the next day,” […]
articles.content:
The explosive documentary NAZA has become a worldwide box office sensation, earning $15 million to date. But if co-directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor had prevailed, it might have gone straight from its Venice Film Festival premiere to The Guardian website.

"At first me and Rachel thought, let's put it out online the next day," Abraham explained as he appeared for a panel discussion about the film at International Documentary Festival Amsterdam ( IDFA ). Their partners on the project convinced the filmmakers that a theatrical release should be part of how NAZA reached viewers. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"It's different audiences," commented Fionualla Jamison, managing director of sales agent-distributor mk2. "Online — it's not necessarily everyone who's going to be aware, who has that viewing habit to go watch something on The Guardian website or on YouTube, depending what people's setups are. So, we felt it was something that could absolutely exist alongside for different audiences and at cinemas." "Our North Star always has been how we're going to get this film to people," said Lindsay Poulton, head of documentaries at The Guardian, who produced the film alongside The Guardian's Harry Davies and James Wilson of JW Films. "I think sitting in a cinema has been an important part of that. We've talked publicly as well about how the film is going to be available on our platform."

Poulton and fellow panelists reiterated The Guardian intends to make the film available for free on its website in early December, although a specific date hasn't been revealed. In the meantime, the documentary has played theatrically in 50 countries, and recorded a remarkable 1.6 million admissions .

Abraham, part of the Oscar-winning quartet of directors of No Other Land , along with Szor, became a believer in the theatrical component. Appearing on the panel by remote from The Guardian offices in London, he said he realized, "The film being immediately accessible doesn't necessarily translate to maximum impact. There is something to be gained from also doing this theatrical run." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

NAZA presents interviews with 24 anonymous members of Israeli intelligence and Israel Defense Forces personnel who describe how Israeli military leaders callously disregarded the potential loss of Palestinian civilian life as they pursued Hamas targets in Gaza. The whistleblowers claim this included deliberating striking Hamas militants at night in their homes with full knowledge those attacks would likely lead to the deaths of innocent women and children. The IDF has denied violating human rights standards and the Geneva Convention in its prosecution of the war. It has also denied an assertion in the film that the IDF used AI to select targets.

The release of NAZA has triggered furor within Israel's right-wing. The country's Culture Minister, Miki Zohar, vowed to strip Abraham and Szor of their Israeli citizenship , a move later endorsed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu . Supporters of the Israeli government went so far as to quickly produce a counter documentary titled NAZA: The Real Story , mimicking the style of Abraham and Szor's film by shooting it on rooftops at night in Tel Aviv.

"There's a film out there that's very misleading. Obviously, it's not a coincidence," Abraham stated. "They call themselves NAZA . They're trying to mislead people into thinking that they are the real NAZA film."

The director also told the audience at the DeLaMar Theater venue at IDFA that Israel's military has released "this kind of guidebook for commanders giving them instructions or explaining to them how to speak with their soldiers about NAZA . So, it's like for commanders in the Israeli Air Force and other officers sort of an explanation as to how you can deal with the claims that are raised in the film. And of course, they say what you'd expect them to say. And very high up it says that the purpose of this guidebook is to strengthen the soldier's sense of the — they use this term ‘righteousness of the path, that what we are doing is right.'"

Abraham said he didn't view the existence of the guidebook or the counter documentary in wholly negative terms.

"There's also something positive about it which I think when you get people to be so defensive, when commanders feel a need to get this kind of guidebook to reassure their soldiers that the path is right and that the army is moral and immune from criticism and that they say NAZA [a Hebrew acronym meaning collateral damage], it's not a bad term," he noted. "There's something also about being defensive, which is a reflection of the sense that you are scrutinized, the sense that you are under magnifying glass… They feel like they're not only watching, they're also being watched. They're not only surveilling in a sense; they're also being surveilled or looked at. And that's good."

James Wilson, the Oscar-nominated producer ( Zone of Interest ) said the message of NAZA won't be derailed by efforts at misinformation.

"It's about horror. It's about mass murder that our society, the West, has been completely implicit in," he insisted. "It couldn't be about something more important and serious and sort of abyssal in its horror… It's like an alarm. It's a fucking alarm and we all have to bear witness to that as it's happening."

Abraham concluded by saying, "People talk about films changing the world. I don't think that a film can really do that, but I think films can definitely, as Jim [Wilson] was saying, they can definitely be part of a network, of a larger kind of energy that exists in the world, which is pushing for change, which is pushing for humanity and empathy."

articles.title: Mark Ruffalo, Tilda Swinton, Michael Moore, Barry Jenkins and More Rally to the Defense of Iranian Filmmaker Jafar Panahi
articles.summary: The heads of Venice and Berlin film festivals as well as actors such as Mark Ruffalo and Tilda Swinton, and directors like Michael Moore, Barry Jenkins and Alex Gibney are among a host of prominent film players who have rallied to the defense of Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi. A statement shared with Variety, so far […]
articles.content:
The heads of Venice and Berlin film festivals as well as actors such as Mark Ruffalo and Tilda Swinton , and directors like Michael Moore, Barry Jenkins and Alex Gibney are among a host of prominent film players who have rallied to the defense of Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi .

A statement shared with Variety , so far signed by 200 individuals or institutions, states that they are "deeply concerned" by reports of the new prison sentence of five years and one month issued by the Tehran Revolutionary Court against Panahi, as well as the confiscation of his assets, the freezing of his bank accounts, a two-year travel ban and a two-year social media ban. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Benjamín Vicuña, Star of Netflix Hit Series 'Envious,' Joins ‘My Last Stand' by Goya-Winner Matías Bize 'Woman Unknown' Breakout Mathilde Arcel on Her Venice Award-Winning Performance and Life After Her Lido Triumph: 'Everything Is Open'

It notes that in December, Iran issued a sentence against Panahi of one year in prison and a two-year ban on leaving the country. It adds that in March, Panahi "courageously decided to return to Iran, aware of the risks but having always spoken of his deep love for his country, and for his desire to stay and work there."

The statement, which was instigated by the International Coalition for Filmmakers at Risk in collaboration with a group of filmmaker in the U.S. and Europe, follows a similar letter of protest published by Cannes on Tuesday that said the festival "condemns the judicial persecution of Jafar Panahi and calls for the lifting of all restrictions that prevent him from traveling, creating and expressing himself freely."

Other filmmakers to add their names to the latest statement of protest include Kleber Mendonça Filho, Laura Poitras, Rithy Panh, Lucrecia Martel, Liz Garbus, Asif Kapadia, Jacques Audiard, Olivier Assayas, Roger Ross Williams, Catherine Breillat, Dominik Moll and Abigail Disney, as well as actor-writer-director Arthur Harari. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

As well as Alberto Barbera at Venice and Tricia Tuttle at Berlinale, other festival chiefs to sign the statement include Locarno's Giona Nazzaro, Rotterdam's Vanja Kaludjercic, New York's Dennis Lim, Telluride's Julie Huntsinger, Karlovy Vary's Karel Och and IDFA's Isabel Arrate Fernandez.

The statement lists some of Panahi's most acclaimed works, such as "The White Balloon" (1995), winner of Cannes' Caméra d'Or, "The Circle" (2000), winner of Venice's Golden Lion, "Offside" (2006), winner of Berlin's Silver Bear, "Taxi" (2015), winner of Berlin's Golden Bear, "No Bears" (2022), winner of Venice's Special Jury Prize, and "It Was Just an Accident" (2025), which won Cannes' Palme d'Or.

It then states, "His films have bridged critical gaps in understanding between the world and the Iranian people for the last 30 years."

It adds, "Mr. Panahi's work matters so much precisely because of his commitment to continue to make films that reveal the beauty and diversity of a culture that has been largely hidden from the rest of the world for close to half a century. In the tradition of great Iranian cinema, his films have kept Iran and Iranians present in the world's imagination in the darkest of times, despite all the pressures exerted on him to be silent."

The statement concludes, "We stand in solidarity with Mr. Panahi and all Iranians facing persecution for their work at the hands of their own government. We call on the Tehran Revolutionary Court to rescind all actions to penalize and imprison Mr. Panahi and to abide by the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights to which the Iranian government is a signatory.

"In this exceptionally heightened moment of conflict and political tension, such artists as Mr. Panahi, who create understanding within and across borders are of utmost importance. The international creative community stands together here to bear witness and to protect freedom of artistic expression everywhere."

Harry Styles , Billie Eilish and Sam Fender are to headline Glastonbury 2027, making them the festival's youngest headliners of the 21st century.

The three solo singers will lead the biggest UK festival, coming after a fallow year in 2026. The 2025 edition was helmed by The 1975, Neil Young and Olivia Rodrigo.

articles.title: The Worst Star Wars Release of All Time Turns 48, But Even The Mandalorian Still Referenced It
articles.summary: Fans of Star Wars are known for both the good and, bad as they can be passionate, overtly negative about new things, and disagreeable, yet they all seem to at least share one opinion, which is about the worst entry in the franchise. A film like Star Wars: The Last Jedi, which is despised by […]
articles.content:
The widespread success of the original film in 1977 meant that people wanted more Star Wars as soon as possible. So, in 1978, two years before The Empire Strikes Back , we got The Star Wars Holiday Special broadcast on TV. It brought back the original cast, introduced one of the most popular characters in the franchise, and yet was met with negative reviews from basically everyone. However, despite its standing as the low point of the series, it has gained cult status over the years and even got referenced in the biggest modern Star Wars hit, The Mandalorian .

On paper, The Star Wars Holiday Special is just a simple good time. It follows the events of the original film and takes place on Kashyyyk, the Wookiee home planet of fan favorite Chewbacca. Simply getting to explore more of this universe is enough to warrant a special like this, especially since we got to see what the world of Wookiees was like and understand more about Chewbacca. The heroes were there to celebrate Life Day, yet they ended up getting pursued by agents of the Empire.

That might sound like a fine little adventure but the reception to the special was immediately negative. The Star Wars Holiday Special was named the dumbest event in television history by David Hofstede, who called it the worst two hours of TV ever. It also sits at a mere 25% on Rotten Tomatoes, which is easily the lowest number for a Star Wars project. George Lucas, who wasn't significantly involved, was unhappy with the finished product, while the cast has also had unpleasant things to say about it.

Harrison Ford has admitted that he has never seen it and didn't even acknowledge the special at first. Mark Hamill has also admitted that he never watched it in full, while Carrie Fisher said she received a rare copy of it from George Lucas (the special famously never received a home video release) so she could put it on at parties when she wanted people to leave. Anthony Daniels, the longtime voice of C-3PO , called the special a “turd” in his autobiography. All that said, the project has become popular with fans for its wackiness and the holiday theme, though even those who enjoy it still consider it the low point of Star Wars history.

Despite the negative reception to The Star Wars Holiday Special , it remains canon. The most notable element of it is the debut of Boba Fett, who went on to become a hugely popular character in The Empire Strikes Back and eventually received his own disappointing show, The Book of Boba Fett . The animated segment is short, yet remains the high point of The Star Wars Holiday Special . The special has also gotten referenced more as time has gone on, including in the premiere episode of The Mandalorian in 2019. It's only a quick nod at first, but the show mentions Life Day on Kashyyyk.

On top of that, The Mandalorian also features a gunfighter who uses a weapon that is clearly the same as the one that Boba Fett used in the animated segment of the special (or is at least a reference to it). While The Mandalorian is the most prominent part of the franchise to bring up The Star Wars Holiday Special , it is far from alone. For starters, several novels feature Chewbacca's family members, who were introduced in this special, while games like Star Wars: Galaxies and Star Wars: The Old Republic explore Kashyyyk and Life Day.

There was even a Life Day comic book released in 2021 and one of the newest Disney+ shows, Star Wars: Skeleton Crew , includes a nod through a hologram circus that is similar to what Lumpy used in The Star Wars Holiday Special . The project has also been referenced in pop culture by Community, The Big Bang Theory , and Weird Al Yankovic. James Gunn even cited it as inspiration for The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special . Thanks to nods in pop culture and The Mandalorian , interest in The Star Wars Holiday Special has grown, leading to a 2023 Disney+ documentary on the making of it.

Do you have a soft spot for The Star Wars Holiday Special or do you hate it? Discuss your feelings on it in the comments!

articles.content:
The Indian adaptation of Universal Television's medical drama “ House ,” starring Nawazuddin Siddiqui as a brilliant but difficult diagnostician, will premiere Dec. 11 on JioHotstar under the title “ Dr. Hassan .”

Dia Mirza co-stars in the show, directed by Rohan Sippy, with a cast that also includes Faisal Rashid, Rehmat Rattan, Jayson Thaam and Smaran Sanu. Siddiqui's character is an unconventional doctor with a knack for solving baffling cases and an eccentric streak to match. When a medical mystery has stumped everyone else, Hassan is the one people call on, though his quirks make him as hard to predict as the illnesses he treats. JioHotstar is positioning the show as more than a standard hospital drama, mixing puzzling cases with humor and friction between its characters.

Siddiqui recalled time spent as a child around the clinics and dispensaries of his hometown. “There were always such interesting people and situations unfolding there. Some of those memories came back to me when I read ‘Dr. Hassan.' What I enjoyed about playing him was finding the balance between his exceptional intelligence and his very particular way of looking at the world,” he said.

Vinay Chhawal and Ketan Pedgaonkar adapted and wrote the series, with dialogue by Virat Basoya. Deepak Dhar, Rishi Negi, Rajesh Chadha, Mrinalini Jain and Shyam Rathi are producers, and Vibhas Singh Gautam is executive producer for Banijay Asia. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“Great characters travel, but they truly come alive when they are rooted in the world of the audience watching them. ‘House' gave the world one of television's most unforgettable characters, and with ‘Dr. Hassan,' we wanted to reimagine that spirit through an Indian lens, with its own humor and humanity,” said Alok Jain, head of Hindi and English entertainment business (streaming, TV and studios) at JioStar.

“Dr. Hassan” is the third international version of “House,” after adaptations in Russia and Turkey. It is also the latest show NBCUniversal Formats and Banijay Asia have co-produced in India, following “Mistry,” the local take on “Monk,” and “Million Dollar Listing India,” which has had two seasons.

Dhar, founder and CEO of Banijay Asia and Endemol Shine India, said the company had approached the Indian version with care, given the show's global fan base. “At its heart is a truly singular character: sharp, flawed, often difficult, and impossible to ignore. Bringing him to life needed a creative team and cast that could balance gripping medical mysteries with wit and emotional depth, and Nawazuddin is an actor who brings real depth to everything he does,” Dhar said.

Created by David Shore, the original “House” starred Hugh Laurie and ran for eight seasons on Fox between 2004 and 2012. Heel and Toe Films, Shore Z Productions, Bad Hat Harry Productions and Universal Television produced the series, which picked up five Primetime Emmys, two Golden Globes, a Peabody and nine People's Choice Awards. Katie Jacobs, Shore, Paul Attanasio, Bryan Singer and Dan Sackheim were executive producers.

Linfield Ng, VP of format sales and production at NBCUniversal Formats, said the company was pleased to be working with Banijay Asia and JioHotstar once again. “With an exceptional cast and creative team, we're excited to see this latest adaptation offer a fresh perspective on a globally loved series,” Ng said.

The India titles form part of a wider push across Asia for NBCUniversal Formats, which had 39 seasons on air in 17 territories in 2025.
